title: Engineering AI Discover
abstract: The challenges and decisions behind AI Discover’s intelligence layer By Varun Khaitan , Peng Ren , Gary Tang , Itay Teller , Atif Faheem , Nipun Kumar , Donnie DeBoer , Eduardo Lundgren , Matteo Rinaldi , Raghav Bakshi We recently introduced AI Discover , a new tab in our TV app where a small group of members can try new ways to find something to watch. For years, our recommendations have worked in the background, inferring what a member might enjoy from their viewing history. AI Discover moves from that silent ranking toward steerable discovery. A member picks a theme, say “Quick Watches,” and gets a row of matching titles, a short note on why they fit and a few narrower themes to try next. From there, they can keep narrowing, head somewhere new or tune what they see. Building AI Discover raised a question many teams will recognize: how do you deliver a better member experience with generative AI on TV without sacrificing speed, reliability or safety? Our answer is a new intelligence layer, the agent harness behind AI Discover. For each request, it decides how to combine LLMs with our recommendation systems. It builds on years of work understanding what members enjoy, and on our recent work applying LLMs to recommendations and generative experiences. The layer itself plans each request, runs it across those systems, serves the result and evaluates it offline. This post covers the challenges we designed for and the key decisions we made along the way. Why an intelligence layer? Every Netflix page combines recommendations with rules. We pick titles a member may enjoy, and eligibility, maturity and safety rules decide what can appear. An experience built on LLMs needs the same rules, plus code that decides when to call an LLM and how to handle its output. That code is called an agent harness, and it’s the core of our intelligence layer. The simplest implementation hands the entire request to an LLM and lets it pick the titles, write the labels and decide what happens next. However, that leaves us relying on probabilistic output where we need governed results, because every turn in AI Discover ends on a screen in someone’s living room. At our scale, even rare failures happen many times a day. A member sees every slow call, unavailable title or off-brand line. Seven challenges shaped our design: Fitting LLMs into a product and architecture designed without them. Traditional recommenders rank titles based on past behavior. LLMs can do more: understand what a member is asking for and plan how to respond. Our existing experience would leave most of that unused. Keeping recommendations grounded. Every pick must be a real, available title from our changing catalog. Retrieval and rankers work in tandem with LLMs to choose titles that fit the member’s taste and intent. Working with slow, unpredictable LLMs. LLM calls are the slowest and most expensive part of the system. Tail latencies can spike, and the output may not be what you asked for. So we use LLMs selectively, treat what they return as untrusted input and test performance and quality before anything ships. Adapting to fast-changing models, tools and prompts. Modeling and engineering solutions keep evolving, so the product can’t depend on any single model, tool or prompt. Building for TV. Typing on a TV is hard, so members rely on the remote, and the app should respond to every press right away on widely varying hardware. TV apps also update slowly, so changes have to ship without an app release. A typical TV request returns in moments, while multi-step generation can take several seconds. Holding a safety and reliability bar at scale. Members always get a page, even when an LLM call fails or yields poor results. Their choices and our content standards hold on every request, and when something breaks, structured records show why. Learning from what members say alongside what we already know. title: De-identifying text at scale: How Airbnb protects personal data in AI training
abstract: Here’s how Airbnb detects and replaces personal data in messages, reviews, and support chats before it reaches a model. By: Emelin Flores , Alex Klimov , Lee Formyduval , Bahador Nooraei Introduction Airbnb is built on trust. Every night that a guest books a stay, or a host welcomes someone into their home, that trust is backed by information they’ve shared with us, which includes personally identifiable information (PII) such as names, home location, current location, and payment details. We now use transaction information to train machine learning models. Before we do so, we remove PII to minimize the number of copies of this information and prevent leakage into and through our models. As we’ve written before , Airbnb maintains a shared taxonomy as to what constitutes PII, from commonly used fields such as names and card numbers to less frequently used fields such as precise location coordinates. We use de-identification to remove PII and replace it with simulated data that’s as realistic as possible to maximize its usefulness for ML model training. Decisions relating to user privacy start as policy. These policies are set and maintained by Airbnb’s Privacy Architecture team, with engagement from Legal, Policy, and Engineering. Engineering then implements policy decisions as code. This post focuses on text de-identification. We’ll describe the OSS library we chose to start with, the changes we made to create a functional system for Airbnb, and how we confirm that the system is working. 1. Choosing Presidio as the foundation Many organizations are concerned with protecting PII, so there’s a lot of existing best practice and tested code out there that we can use. We chose Presidio , an open-source library originally developed by Microsoft and recently transitioned to community governance. We needed to meet demanding requirements: On-premises hosting, to keep data on our infrastructure General-purpose functionality and high degree of modularity, for maximum extensibility Multilingual support, for our global user base PII detection and obfuscation separate, but within a single framework, for manageability and consistency Support for redaction, masking, and realistic replacement Consistent fake values within a run (ie, the same name repeatedly produces the same fake result) Presidio meets these requirements well, especially regarding modularity. Functional elements such as PII recognizers, natural language processing (NLP) engines, and operators are all pluggable. We bypassed alternatives such as managed cloud services, since hosting is not on-premises, and standalone recognizers, known as named entity recognition (NER) models, since they only address part of the problem we needed to solve. 1.1 Deployment and distribution Presidio ships as a Python package , and each consumer imports it in-process rather than calling a service we operate. Raw personal data is de-identified inside the calling process, so no separate service holds it and the data flow stays simple. It also removes a central bottleneck, since jobs run independently wherever compute is available. The decision is reversible: the same library wraps into a service if the need arises. The tradeoff is distribution. The library only protects data if every pipeline calls it, on the current version, with a compliant configuration. Models at Airbnb train through a shared machine learning (ML) workflow orchestrator, so the library ships as a reusable pipeline step. A team supplies only its data schema, marking which columns carry personal data; we own the recognizers, operators, language handling, and runtime environment. The resulting dataset is tagged as de-identified, and that tag follows the data into the model registry, where it is designed to gate deployment to production. Each run records the library version and configuration used, so registered models can be traced back to the datasets that produced them. The Value of Human Expertise in The Software Factory
abstract: “Any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic.” – Arthur C. Clarke Most developers now write less code by hand. Gergely Orosz recently posted that modern software engineering is no longer done without LLMs and will no longer be done without them. Some miss writing code, while others question how much of the code that agents produce should be read. Writing and reading code gave a lot of developers satisfaction and identity, and as Kent Beck has put it , a sense of competence. I saw this in real time. Ten years ago, I’d sit at conferences and feel a sense of wonder whenever anyone was brave enough to do a live demo. I felt gleeful when they wrote lines of code, went back to fix mistakes, and made something cool and interesting appear on the screen in front of me. It was magical, and I’m sure that magic is why a lot of developers got into this industry. I can partly understand the sense of loss that people are experiencing. I saw magic, they were in charge of the craft of their code, and that hands-on task has now been given to agents. Where does that expertise go when AI is now writing so much of the code? As Tim O’Reilly wrote in his recent Radar post , O’Reilly is a business built on cultivating and sharing human expertise. Our job is to find the high ground where that expertise still matters. For developers working in a new world of agentic software factories, I think the expertise you built writing and maintaining software hasn’t gone, it’s just moved. Your expertise now shapes how agents produce software and what evidence you need before we trust the result. To me, AI is enabling you to be magical faster . Agents amplify whatever you give them, but you need to understand it in the first place. I couldn’t swarm a fleet of agents in the same way a developer can because I don’t have the expertise. You need to understand code. The expertise has gone to a new level of abstraction. When I spoke recently with Avi Flombaum, the founder of Flatiron School, he agreed that developers’ value was never solely in writing or reading code. AI changes the mechanics, but experience still matters for understanding complex problem domains, articulating what needs to be built, and bringing judgment and ambition to the work. In a separate conversation with Ken Kousen, he pointed out, “We’ve been working with third-party code generators for years; we just called it outsourcing.” This new world of designing AI workflows, setting guardrails, and managing agents much as you would an engineering team, reveals a chance to use accumulated expertise more. It’s your software engineering expertise that matters. Software factories make this shift especially visible. Companies are now putting agents to work across the development lifecycle, aiming to take work from an initial signal through implementation, validation, and deployment without a person at every step. But generating more code is only part of that process. Without changes elsewhere, you can burn a lot of tokens producing a pile of pull requests that someone still has to review. Anthropic’s AI-native SDLC playbook points out that speeding up implementation shifts pressure onto planning, testing, review, handoffs and approvals, and faster coding tools don’t speed those up on their own. Someone has to understand the whole process well enough to redesign it. In a software factory, that judgment has to be built into the system. Humans design the workflow, define the conditions under which work can proceed, and decide which exceptions need their attention. Anthropic reports that Claude authors about 80% of the code merged into its codebase, alongside a review process that combines automated checks with human oversight according to risk. The state of the code matters too. title: When AI-Generated Data Becomes Tomorrow’s Ground Truth
abstract: Manufacturers qualify suppliers before trusting them with critical work. Before a supplier can provide parts for a regulated product such as a medical device, the manufacturer collects evidence: quality certifications, test reports, insurance documents, and regulatory approvals. Increasingly, an AI agent reads that evidence first. The agent reviews the documents and proposes a finding, and a business process decides whether the finding is good enough for the supplier to be accepted. Once a supplier is accepted, that decision is recorded in the manufacturer’s supplier-management system. From there, sourcing workflows, readiness dashboards, and program reports all rely on that record without repeating the review. Here is how that process can go wrong. A supplier-review agent examines a new supplier’s documents and concludes that a mandatory quality certificate is valid. The qualification workflow accepts the finding, the supplier is recorded as compliant, and the procurement lead approves the supplier for an upcoming order. A few days later, a human reviewer notices that the certificate does not cover the part being sourced; the agent had misread the certificate’s scope. At 11:00am, the reviewer corrects the supplier record and sends the supplier back for review. At 2:00pm, the readiness dashboard still shows the supplier as cleared, and a program report still lists the supplier as compliant. The procurement lead’s sourcing decision remains in force, and nothing tells the procurement lead that the evidence behind it has changed. A misread scope is only one way a certificate finding can fail. A certificate may be revoked after it was checked, expire before the order ships, apply to a different plant than the one making the part, or turn out to be forged. In each case, someone can correct the supplier record while the systems that already used the old finding keep acting on it. No system in this example malfunctioned. Each one processed information that appeared valid under its local contract, yet the combined result was wrong. The manufacturer had corrected a value without correcting its influence. Part of this is a familiar problem: Enterprise systems have always struggled to keep reports, indexes, caches, and workflow state in line with the source record. Agents make the problem harder because they generate conclusions. A conclusion can be assembled from several sources, rewritten in reports, and retrieved later as if it were independent evidence. Reconciliation can make stored values agree. It cannot reveal that differently worded records come from the same conclusion, or find the decisions that already relied on that conclusion. This problem is not limited to manufacturing. In our work across banking, telecommunications, and resources, it appears wherever an agent’s output becomes a record that other systems trust. A fraud classification is written into a case record. A risk assessment is summarized in a management report. An incident diagnosis becomes part of a knowledge base. In each of these cases, as in the supplier example, the conclusion loses some of its original context at every step it passes through and begins to influence decisions made later. The conclusion can also travel back into model development. Accepted findings become labeled examples, evaluation sets, and fine-tuning data, where they are treated as ground truth for the next model. If an incorrect supplier finding survives correction in the operational systems, a future model may learn it. Whether the conclusion ends up in a dashboard, a report, or a training set, the hard problem is the same: finding every consequential decision that depends on a result that can change. title: The Monday Morning Agent: Are Kickers Too Good Now?
abstract: “Kickers are too good now” sounds plausible when long field goals keep making the highlights. But in the November 9 episode of The Monday Morning Agent , our AI analyst found that long kicks went through at roughly the same rate across the seasons on file. Coaches were attempting them more often. We gave the agent written visualization standards so its charts would show both success rates and attempts per game, with the context readers need to judge the claim. Decide how to draw the trend before seeing the answer We started with two charts of league-wide field goal success rates. One began in 2024, with a vertical axis starting around 84%. The line climbed to 85.6%, and the improvement looked dramatic. The other included every season from 2021 onward, started the vertical axis at zero, and showed the attempt count beneath each point. Success rates stayed around 84% to 86%. The recent rise looked much smaller in that context. Changing the starting year and axis made the recent improvement look larger. Before your agent draws a trend, decide which choices it can make. Otherwise, it can produce a persuasive picture without giving readers the context to assess it. Keep the definitions when you add a new capability The dictionary from episode two still applies. During a rehearsal, that earlier agent refused the kicking claim because its dictionary could describe a rush but couldn’t describe a kick. We expanded what it could define while keeping the requirement to use a saved definition. This time, the play descriptions named field goals and included distances. We still had to decide where “long” starts. A recognizable play name doesn’t settle how to group it for analysis. We examined distance bands separately. Kickers made roughly 95% of attempts under 40 yards. Success rates hovered around 80% for attempts from 40 to 49 yards and around 70% for those from 50 to 59 yards. Combining them into one rate can hide the differences the question asks about. Make the chart standard specific enough to enforce We introduced eight rules. Every trend includes all seasons on file, and axes start at zero. Each point shows its underlying count. Yellow identifies the subject of the claim, blue identifies the comparison, and gray marks the current season. The chart title asks a question rather than announcing a conclusion. A source line gives the exact command that produced the data, so readers can rerun it. The chart shows only values the tool printed, without added trend lines or numbers typed by hand. Every chart uses the same layout, with success rates above attempts per game. Writing these standards down gives the agent consistent instructions and gives readers a familiar way to compare results across episodes. Choose standards that fit your analysis, then specify how you’ll check each one. Test a chart that breaks the rules A written standard needs a way to enforce it. We added a renderer, the program that turns the agent’s chart specification into a picture. It checks the chart specification against the rules before drawing the chart and refuses specifications that break them. We deliberately requested a trend beginning in 2023. The renderer refused because the first season on file was 2021. Its response identified the rule instead of producing the shortened chart. Give your agent a request that violates a standard and inspect the response. That check shows whether the restriction works when the agent tries to produce an output. Show how much evidence sits behind each rate The longest kicks need particular care. The episode’s current-season sample contained only nine attempts in the group of kicks from 60 yards or farther. The next kick could noticeably change that rate. Displaying counts beside percentages helps readers distinguish a small sample from hundreds of attempts. title: When AI Can Code, What Is Left for Programmers to Do?
abstract: AI is in such widespread use for programming that project maintainers (particularly for free and open source software) are complaining about the burden of reviewing mounds of low-quality code. In fact, AI can help with every stage of code development: writing the specification, coding, uncovering bugs, and repairing the code. This article describes human-AI collaboration at specification and code repair stages, and lays out the skills that humans need to accomplish those tasks in the current generation of AI. We won’t cover coding and bug finding because they are widely discussed elsewhere. Let the AI harness write the spec We don’t want developers hand-writing specs. We want them in a room, or on a call, talking with the product manager (PM) and the customer. Humans reach a limit when writing. We skip the boring cases. We get tired by requirement 40. We use “customer” on page 1 and “client” on page 6 of the spec. We write down what we remember and forget what we assumed. AI has the patience and diligence we lack. It’s still up to human developers to write guardrails or constraints into the spec: statements to ensure that nothing wildly wrong makes it into code. Each guardrail should be one sentence that says MUST or MUST NOT, with a proof beside it: a test, a check, or a named person who reviews it. A guardrail with no proof is a wish. Write the guardrails first, because the PM won’t think of most of them. What must never happen? Who must never see this? What should the agent never touch? With guardrails in place, capture the conversation and let the machine do the writing. Two AI tools have shown themselves particularly useful to analyze requirements: The Plaud Note recorder attaches to the back of your phone and records in-person conversations and phone calls; the wearable NotePin records in-person conversations, not phone calls. Granola runs on your laptop or phone, uses your computer’s audio, and analyzes what it captures. We find these products to be a leap above common AI tools for summarizing conversations, when it comes to specification development. Plaud and Granola (if you prompt them to do so) can notice what’s missing and tell you the gaps in the requirements. They ask, What happens when this field is empty? What if two people do this at once? Who is allowed to see it? over and over, for every requirement, and check each noun in the requirements against an ontology created by the programmer (often with the help of AI). The developer, the PM, and the customer read the output from the AI, fix what’s wrong, answer what’s missing, and go through the process again. The spec that comes out of that loop tends to be more complete and more consistent than what the same people write alone. That’s Shahid’s own experience, not a study, but it matches reports from some other people at the leading edge of the use of AI for software development. Mark Pike, a product lawyer at Anthropic, builds working tools for his legal team without writing code: “ I just typed a normal sentence, describing what I wanted. And it worked .” StrongDM, which runs a software factory where agents write and test the code, says the starting point for a piece of software can be “ a few sentences, a screenshot, or an existing codebase .” Keep the spec after the feature ships. As you prepare a new version of the product next year, it can tell you why the code looks the way it does. The data schema is the other half of the spec Most teams treat the data schema as plumbing. Tables get named by whoever got there first. The spec, reflecting human conversation, may say customer , account , client , and org at different places for the same thing, and you have to choose one noun for the schema. A human learns the mapping by sitting next to the person who wrote it. An AI agent has no neighbor to consult, so it guesses—with results that likely differ from Monday to Tuesday. title: Understanding Positional Embeddings in Modern LLMs
abstract: This article explains how LLMs encode and process token position information by covering classic and contemporary methods like RoPE. It’s essentially a comprehensive journey where we will work through the mechanisms with visual examples, a little math, and a small PyTorch implementation. And, of course, we will then also look at how modern architectures adapt or omit explicit positional encodings. Below, you can find a preview of which positional embedding choices are used in 2026 open-weight models. We will discuss these choices later after covering the underlying mechanisms. Figure 1: A preview of the gallery’s 2026 architectures, grouped by positional encoding. Architecture figures taken from my LLM gallery . But why spending so much time writing/reading about this rather minor building block? LLMs keep evolving, and as I was preparing a new article on the latest LLM architecture trends this year, I realized that I never covered the positional information methods used in LLMs in any article so far. So, instead of letting the other article get out of hand, I thought it might make sense to publish this as a standalone building block for the upcoming LLM architecture and trends analysis. Also, over the years, many readers have asked me for a tutorial on relative positional embeddings (aka RoPE) to follow up on the learned absolute embeddings used in GPT. It’s been on my TODO list for a long time, so I finally revisited my old draft and put this walkthrough together, which will cover different positional methods in LLMs; (finally) how RoPE works; what methods are used by recent open LLMs. Note that this article assumes some familiarity with basic LLM architectures and works well as a follow-up to Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch) . If the concepts and computation of the attention internals, particularly query, key, and value vectors, are a little fuzzy, I recommend checking my self-attention walkthrough as a refresher: The article is also very technical and likely too detailed for some. However, I really wanted to have this foundation out there for future articles to reference. And no worries, the next one will return to a more comfortable style. PS: I started experimenting with Substack’s new “perks” system. As a thank-you to supporters, I’ve added image exports and metadata from the architecture gallery for you to use in your own analyses. PPS: If you are already familiar with how position embeddings work, feel free to fast-forward to Section 6, Positional choices in modern architectures . Note that this article may be best read in a web browser than an email client. I recommend checking out the web view here , which also has a navigation bar on the left side. 1. Where position information enters an LLM Let’s start with the overall architecture. A tokenizer encodes the input text into token IDs. Next, the input token embedding layer of an LLM maps each of these IDs to a vector of numbers. We usually refer to these entries in that vector as “features” (similar to classic ML). The transformer blocks inside the LLM then modify these vectors using attention and feedforward layers. Lastly, the model’s output layer produces logit scores (converted into probabilities) for the next token. The following shows this path in GPT-2 (a relatively classic LLM) and MiniMax-M3 (a more recent LLM released this year; a placeholder for most other recent LLMs). As we can see, the architectures are not too different from each other, but before we get to the positional information parts, let’s focus on the orange blocks for now (the token embedding layers) and the transformer blocks above them; the other architecture differences aren’t needed for this explanation. title: Hydropower hit record lows in the US Southwest this summer
abstract: The US Southwest generated 28% less electricity via hydropower between April and August than the 10-year average, according to new data from the US Energy Information Administration. Most hydropower plants in the US rely on dams to hold back water, creating reservoirs. The water can be released through turbines, generating electricity on demand. But an extreme, prolonged drought in the Colorado River Basin has resulted in dangerously low water levels in the Southwest’s two largest reservoirs, affecting the availability of this power source. Residents and farmers in the US Southwest, a region that includes Arizona, New Mexico, and parts of Nevada and California, rely on water that melts in the spring from snowpack in the mountains and is slowly allowed to flow south via dam releases. Snowfall in the Rocky Mountains provides about 85% of the annual flow of the Colorado River . And in recent years, the river has seen record-low flows. Two reservoirs along the Colorado River, Lake Powell and Lake Mead, have struggled to stay above the minimum level required for hydropower plants. At the end of September, Lake Powell’s depth was 3,518 feet, less than 1% above the level required to run the water through turbines that produce electricity at the Glen Canyon power plant. The Hoover Dam power plant requires 950 feet in Lake Mead, and that reservoir was 9% above the minimum in September. Together, the two plants produced nearly seven terawatt-hours of electricity in 2025, enough to serve over 2 million people. Low water levels have been an ongoing struggle for the region, which has been in a drought for 27 years. Meanwhile, climate change is continuing to shift rainfall and snowfall patterns across the region and around the world. The effects of climate change on hydropower aren’t entirely straightforward globally—some regions will see more rain and snow because of shifting weather patterns, while others are likely to see less. But it’s playing a role for hydropower availability, according to one 2022 review study . Rising temperatures bring more droughts, warmer winters means less snow and ice to fill the reservoirs, and more variability in precipitation can lead to alternating floods and droughts, making the power source less reliable. Hydropower production is likely to be at its lowest level in over a decade in 2026 and tick even lower in 2027, according to projections from the EIA. El Niño could provide some temporary relief. Sometimes this weather pattern can mean cooler, wetter conditions for the southern US. Heavy rains brought floods to the region in October and early November, and the water levels in Lake Powell rose more than 20 feet from their mid-September low. But the water is still quite low, and it’ll take much more to help reservoirs recover from decades of drought conditions. Even as a changing climate complicates the availability of hydropower, the decline in capacity could push greenhouse-gas emissions higher. In 2023, energy-related greenhouse-gas emissions rose by 1.1% globally. A worldwide shortfall in hydropower generation accounted for about 40% of that rise, according to a report from the International Energy Agency.

title: The open-source movement wants Jensen Huang back
abstract: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here . On Friday, a petition to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia began circulating on social media, and by Monday it listed some notable signatories, including Elon Musk and several influential Nvidia researchers. But comb through the more than 115,000 names and you’ll notice a significant faction of Huang’s supporters—higher-ups from Hugging Face, a hub for sharing AI models, and venture capital firms Andreessen Horowitz and Sequoia Capital—come from a particular slice of the tech world. These names have a vested interest in the development of open-source AI, models that, unlike ChatGPT or Claude, can be downloaded and run independent of large tech companies. Supporters of such models say that concentrating AI in the hands of a few powerful companies will leave everyone else worse off (a concern that wouldn’t sound out of place among the AI industry’s critics on the left, if so many open-source advocates weren’t also venture capitalists who stand to profit when startups can build on cheaper AI without paying Big Tech). Huang had become a sort of ringleader for those who defend open source to policymakers against concerns that such models come with no guardrails and cede AI leadership to China, where the most powerful and popular open-source models are created. They now want their most influential voice returned to his post. But it’s not just Huang’s extramarital affairs that threaten his (and Nvidia’s) credibility as an advocate for open-source AI. New research into China’s startups using Nvidia’s chips, and a new rule from the US Department of Commerce announced Monday, could deal a blow to both the movement’s reputation and its technical progress. On Thursday, the day Huang resigned, ex-OpenAI researcher Will DePue published findings online suggesting that China’s AI companies had far more access to Nvidia’s advanced Blackwell chips than previously estimated. China is banned from accessing Nvidia’s most cutting-edge chips to help protect America’s AI lead. It’s unclear how they would have gained access to the chips. DePue claims the results were verified by senior researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic, but an independent analysis has not confirmed the results. (DePue did not respond to a request for an interview. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.) The findings do not establish that Nvidia helped Chinese companies obtain the chips, and the broader problem of chip smuggling was already known to extend well beyond Nvidia’s control. But in suggesting that Nvidia may have profited from the rise of Chinese AI startups, whose models are increasingly being used by American companies instead of domestic alternatives, the findings do leave Huang in an awkward position. He has championed open-source AI as a way to strengthen American technological leadership. “Without open source, startups can’t thrive, university researchers can’t do research, you can’t teach AI, scientists can’t use AI,” he said last December during a talk about helping the US win the AI race against China. It also makes the idea of reinstating Huang even more of a long shot. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent even said last week that Nvidia should not consider someone from inside the company to replace him. The new findings lower Huang’s chances further. What happens next? Nvidia announced in September it would acquire Hugging Face for nearly $13 billion. Its support for open source also serves a straightforward financial interest: The more businesses that build their own models instead of forking over money to Anthropic and OpenAI, the more chips Nvidia can sell. But a new rule from the US Department of Commerce could mean the models popular on Hugging Face will soon stop getting smarter. title: Building trustworthy AI by fencing it in, not predicting it
abstract: In October this year, OpenAI disclosed that two of its AI agents had switched off the systems built to monitor them. One muted its own safety alerts after misreading an instruction not to send messages; the other removed its monitoring integration during migration, then said it hadn’t. No rule had told the agents to do that, and no test had anticipated the behaviors. For a century, we have built trust in technology on predictability: predefined inputs, predictable outputs, and layers of protection. Consider how a breaker trips at a set current or an aircraft component is tested against known (i.e., predictable) stresses. AI changes that. Traditional software executes instructions written by humans, whereas AI exercises what might be called synthetic judgment. We use AI because it can interpret situations we did not program and generate responses we did not prescribe. But the more freedom we give AI, the harder it becomes to provide the predictability on which trust has traditionally been built. We will not make AI trustworthy by predicting what it will do. We will do it by fencing it in with hard limits that are enforced outside its reach. In OpenAI’s case, the safeguards sat inside a system the agents could edit. But a fence the agents can simply move is not a fence. Where traditional definitions of trust fall short Recent MIT Technology Review coverage has approached this problem from other directions. One contributor argues that having a human in the loop is an insufficient solution because humans are fundamentally unable to understand AI systems’ intentions and advocates instead for interdisciplinary research and collaboration between academia, government, and the tech industry. And a story on reverse game theory describes using incentives to keep models from deviating from the rules, even when no one understands how they work on the inside. Both articles acknowledge that we cannot understand or watch every AI decision. Our instruments of trust, including requirements, testing, certification, safety margins, interlocks, and pass/fail criteria, all depend on our ability to bound a system’s behavior. This is the determinism paradox. With generative and agentic AI, behavior is shaped by training data, architecture, prompts, context, retrieval sources, and the environment. Inputs change, models are updated, tools change, and agents interact. Small variations propagate into outcomes nobody designed. The problem is not randomness; it is that the space of possible behavior is too large to enumerate in advance. Trust must therefore be engineered around boundaries rather than predicted outputs. The goal is not deterministic AI, but bounded, observable, and controllable AI. Trust also cannot be a one-time test. Traditional assurance certifies a product at a point in time, but AI keeps evolving after deployment, and a system that has passed every test can drift outside the conditions that made those tests meaningful. Trust must be continuously earned. Safety engineering has been accounting for some of this variability for decades. For example, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission determine the likelihood of failures in complex systems, and Systems-Theoretic Accident Model and Processes (STAMP) showed that accidents can emerge from interactions among working components, people, and organizations. But AI raises the stakes, because just a single component can now interpret, infer, and act. The stakes rise further as AI moves from browsers into vehicles, robots, medical systems, industrial controls, and data centers, where a wrong answer can become a life-threatening event. Building trust that scales It’s clear that a person rubber-stamping thousands of AI actions an hour is not an acceptable—or scalable—safeguard against risk. But the remedy is not to remove people from the loop; it is to put human judgment where it counts: setting limits in advance and approving the rare actions that have serious consequences while hard constraints handle

title: Building AI that can work across the enterprise
abstract: For years, enterprises have approached AI as a series of discrete experiments. Now, as AI agents begin to move into the workflows that run the business, that model is starting to look inadequate. Organizations moving from isolated pilots toward AI agents and autonomous workflows are confronting a deeper challenge: rethinking how data, business processes, governance, and people fit together, turning AI from a collection of tools into part of the enterprise operating model. For Thorsten Leiduck, SVP and global head of SAP Business AI Platform Ecosystem, that shift begins with treating AI as an enterprise platform rather than a collection of disconnected projects. “AI is absolutely dependent on the data foundation,” he says, arguing that companies need a connected, semantically rich layer that reflects their business before they can reliably deploy AI across processes. The stakes also change as AI moves into mission-critical workflows. For some everyday applications, “80% might be good enough,” he says, but in areas such as supply chains or financial close, that level of accuracy is “a very terrible result.” That foundation also determines which AI applications are worth pursuing. Satinder Pal Singh, associate VP North America for SAP BAIP and SAP AI Strategy at Infosys, frames AI agents as “digital coworkers” and recommends evaluating potential use cases through three lenses: impact, feasibility, and scalability. Companies should identify where an agent can move meaningful business metrics, determine whether their data and talent can support the use case, and then establish whether successful applications can be replicated. “A pilot that can’t scale is just an experiment,” he says. Scaling also brings governance into sharper focus. Clear policies, access controls, monitoring, and oversight are necessary to ensure agents remain trustworthy and aligned with business requirements. “The absence of governance doesn’t speed up AI adoption,” Singh says. “It creates a risk backlog” that can ultimately force a more disruptive stop and audit. Those considerations will become more important as AI agents take on more responsibilities as digital coworkers. Both executives see a future in which agentic systems coordinate work across applications, while customer-specific knowledge graphs and governed data become critical enterprise assets. For Singh, the longer-term opportunity is a shift from AI as a productivity tool to “AI as a decision-making partner,” helping leaders understand what is happening, anticipate what comes next, and determine how to respond. This episode of Business Lab is produced in partnership with Infosys. Full Transcript Megan Tatum: From MIT Technology Review, I’m Megan Tatum, and this is Business Lab, the show that helps business leaders make sense of new technologies coming out of the lab and into the marketplace. This episode is produced in partnership with Infosys. Now, the development and democratization of AI tools has the potential to reconfigure how enterprises operate. But, at a time when applications are being scaled up from that initial phase of experimentation, we’re still seeing senior leaders grapple with questions around AI’s value, risk, and the complexity it adds. It’s becoming clear that, unlike past ways of automation, AI requires a real mindset shift. Put simply, the technology can’t simply be added into an enterprise’s existing toolkit. It requires a complete reconfiguration of what’s inside and how it’s used. Two words for you: conscious configuration. My guests today are Thorsten Leiduck, SVP and global head of SAP Business AI Platform Ecosystem, and Satinder Pal Singh, Associate VP for North America, SAP Business AI Platform and SAP AI Strategy. title: IEEE Celebrates 10 Years of Incorporating Ethics Into AI Systems
abstract: Policymakers, technologists, and members of the public have raised concerns about the harm AI’s rapid advancement might cause to society. Their concerns include bias, data privacy violations, the spread of misinformation, and losing control of AI agents. Those issues are relatively new to many people, but the IEEE Standards Association has been working for the past decade on ways to prioritize the responsible development of AI systems. In 2016 IEEE SA launched the IEEE Global Initiative for Ethical Considerations in Autonomous and Intelligent Systems (A/IS) and published the Ethically Aligned Design report. EAD ’s mission is to encourage everyone involved in designing autonomous and intelligent systems to prioritize human well-being by applying ethical considerations for the benefit of humanity. Developed by a multidisciplinary community of experts from around the world, the report outlined eight foundational principles for A/IS. They include human rights, people’s well-being, and transparency. More than 100 leading AI ethics experts provided input. EAD ’s Version II report was released in 2017. Both versions solicited public input and received hundreds of pages of feedback, according to John C. Havens , who was the global initiative’s founding executive director, and is now the global director for IEEE Planet Positive 2030 . And by 2019, there were more than 400 contributors and the community continues to grow. “ Ethically Aligned Design was the first of its kind in the sense of a report that was more than a list of principles and from an organization with the credibility of IEEE,” Havens says. “At the time it was released, there wasn’t anything like it.” Since its launch, a series of standards has been developed to provide practical guidelines on designing, building, and deploying technology that prioritizes human values. Several AI ethics certification programs have been introduced. This year marks the 10th anniversary of EAD ’s first draft. To celebrate, IEEE SA recently launched a website , a podcast series , and a blog that reflect on the report’s achievements and impact. Eight guiding principles The word ethics is often used interchangeably with morality , but that is not the case in responsible AI systems design, according to EAD ’s first version. The report includes insights from classical ethics traditions and value-based design methodologies to offer actionable recommendations for engineers developing AI tools. The report established eight foundational general principles for designing autonomous systems: respecting human rights, prioritizing increased well-being as success criteria for development, empowering individuals with data agency to have control over their identity, effectiveness, transparency, accountability, awareness of misuse, and competence for the system creators. The principles shift applied ethics to the design stage of AI systems, compared with being a concern after they’re released, the authors wrote. A suite of standards The IEEE 7000 series of standards has been developed based on EAD ’s framework. Currently the series consists of 29 projects, 11 of which have been published, and more are still being added. They cover topics such as ethical system design model process ( IEEE 7000-2021 ), AI system transparency ( IEEE 7001-2021 ), data privacy ( IEEE 7002-2022 ), algorithmic bias considerations ( IEEE 7003 -2024), the impact on people’s well-being ( IEEE 7010-2020 ), machine-readable personal privacy requirements ( IEEE 7012-2025 ), and systems that mimic human empathy ( IEEE 7014-2024 ). AI ethics certifications IEEE SA offers a suite of ethics in AI programs including IEEE CertifAIEd , which includes two certifications : one for individuals and one for products. title: AI Is Giving Optical Computing Another Shot
abstract: The idea of computing with light has been around for over 70 years, but until recently it’s remained largely in the realm of research. Over the past few years, though, optical computing has emerged as a fast-growing industry: Market valuation of companies in this sector now totals US $2.22 billion, up from $0.4 billion in 2022. One projection suggests that the market will continue to grow exponentially in the coming years. The reason for this sudden surge will surprise no one: AI. In particular, AI inference—the process of using AI models to respond to user queries—has driven much of the construction of huge, power-hungry data centers, and relatively energy-efficient optical systems are seen as a potential way forward. “Most of the interest in [photonics] is driven by the fact that AI inference has literally become limited by power, and in a rather striking manner,” says Peter McMahon , associate professor of applied and engineering physics at Cornell University, in Ithaca, N.Y., who has researched optical computing for over a decade. Optics, at least on paper, carries the promise of doing the same math as today’s GPUs at a drastically lower level of power. Switching from electronics to optics would be a pretty radical solution. Nevertheless, like mushrooms after a rainstorm, optical-computing startups are popping up in the United States, China, Germany, and Israel. And while competing against such GPU makers as Nvidia is an ambitious goal, the investment in optical computing has spurred development of complementary approaches, such as designing alternative AI algorithms, taking on scientific computing, and enhancing in-network computing. Optalysys, based in England, is inserting optical-computing elements into the networking path, where data centers already use light. The company’s basic on-chip optical element, shown in the inset, is a Fourier transform calculator. Optalysys “I think it would be good for the technology if many of these companies made a good run at it,” says Logan Wright , assistant professor of applied physics at Yale University, in New Haven, Conn., and a former postdoc in McMahon’s lab. “I think that the technology that will be developed through this would be really, really useful, and enable photonic systems that maybe don’t get on this wave of AI but would be capable of doing really quite special things.” Optics to inference’s rescue? Inference makes up the bulk of AI energy use. The industry is already spending billions of dollars designing advanced GPUs and other chips to run inference as efficiently as possible. At the heart of the inference computation is one operation, done countless times a second: matrix-vector multiplication. Back in 1978, optical-computing pioneer Joseph W. Goodman and his coworkers proposed a method for doing matrix-vector multiplication with light. The setup was relatively simple. Let’s say a vector of length N needs to be multiplied by a matrix of size N by N . N light-emitting diodes, all in a row, encode the elements of the vector into the intensity of light—the brighter the light from an individual diode, the greater the value that diode encodes. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads out the light vertically, essentially copying the vector N times. The light then passes through an attenuator of N by N pixels. At each pixel, the light is attenuated according to the corresponding value at that location in the matrix. Passing the light through the attenuator performs the multiplication. Finally, a cylindrical lens oriented perpendicular to the first lens re-collects the light from each row, summing it up. The final vector is measured by a row of detectors. VECTOR-MATRIX MULTIPLICATION The most computationally expensive part of common AI today is vector-matrix (or matrix-matrix) multiplication. For a vector of length N (here, N = 3), it takes N 2 (here, 9) multiplication steps and three accumulation steps—multiple additions at once. The argument for why optics might be advantageous

title: AI Companies Develop Decision Models to Avoid Hallucinations
abstract: On 15 September, a startup called TypeSafe AI released a new AI model called Jev . The company’s broad, disruptive claims about Jev that turned heads: The company claimed that Jev, which it calls a “System One model” is cheaper, faster, and can’t hallucinate. TypeSafe AI’s marketing is an obvious shot across the bow of other AI companies and their large language models (LLMs), which, despite their capabilities in math and coding, are infamous for their cost and tendency to “hallucinate” factually incorrect replies. And the startup has certainly attracted both attention and investment. The company recently raised $870 million in funding at a valuation of $7.5 billion . But the most impressive metric of Jev’s success is arguably the many imitators it’s already spawned. Cloudflare, Amazon, OpenAI, and Microsoft quickly released “decision models” that imitate Jev’s capabilities. Start-ups, academic researchers, and independent enthusiasts have released dozens more. “I have to give Jev credit,” says Matt Mastracci , an independent developer who has trained and released several decision models including Djev , which Cloudflare cited as an inspiration for its own decision models . “It really brought decision models to the forefront. In six or seven weeks, we’ve seen dozens of models come out.” Jev’s Latency and Compute Advantages Most AI researchers would call Jev a decision model or decider model. TypeSafe AI’s branding of Jev as a System One model refers to a theory of cognition popularized by psychologist Daniel Kahneman in his book Thinking, Fast and Slow . In the book, Kahneman draws a line between fast, instinctive thought (System One) and slower, deliberate thought (System Two). TypeSafe AI argues that modern LLMs offer the second, but are too slow to provide the first. The company claims that Jev can provide end-to-end response latency between 70 and 500 milliseconds. By comparison, LLMs typically require at least several seconds, to provide a response, and more complicated tasks (like coding software from scratch) can take several hours. Independent testing backs up TypeSafe AI’s claims. A pre-print co-authored by Ramayya Krishnan , a professor of information systems at Carnegie Mellon University, along with several colleagues, found that Jev delivered a median latency of 150 milliseconds across several benchmarks designed to gauge decision accuracy, including RewardBench and JudgeBench . OpenAI’s most capable model at the time, GPT-6 Astra, delivered a median latency of 1.89 seconds. A faster reply is often a cheaper reply, because it requires less compute time, and that’s reflected in TypeSafe AI’s pricing. The startup charges US $0.042 per million input tokens and output tokens are free. By contrast, for GPT-6 Astra, ChatGPT charges $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output tokens. Even GPT-6 Luna, a variant of GPT-6 designed for fast, inexpensive inference, costs $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens . Mastracci says that lower latency and costs open opportunities to tackle tasks LLMs currently can’t handle.“You can think of content moderation, such as moderating a fire hose of social media posts, or an extremely busy chat room.” Michelle Chen , a group product manager at Cloudflare (which has released its own decision models, including Clef and Claric ), is also bullish on what decision models can accomplish. “You can probably offload 80 percent of your typical LLM tasks to a System One model that is going to be so much faster and so much cheaper.” TypeSafe AI has offered few details about how Jev achieves its speed, but Jev’s open-weights imitators provide more transparency. For example, take Cloudflare’s Clef, an open-weights decision model which is free to download on Hugging Face . “With an LLM, when you’re generating an output token, it looks at all the previous tokens, and predicts the next output token,” explains Chen. title: 28 Zero-Day Findings in Under Two Days. Is Robotics Security Keeping Pace?
abstract: This article is brought to you by VicOne . VicOne identified an initial set of 28 zero-day findings in less than two days using AI-assisted research across software and tools supporting the Physical AI ecosystem. These include projects developed or maintained by Google, NVIDIA, and Meta, among others. Based on initial validation, all 28 findings are classified as zero-day vulnerabilities. The count may change following vendor and vulnerability-authority review, and some findings do not yet have CVE tracking numbers. Many of these tools help teams train, simulate, test, and operate robots. Weaknesses in them could influence the models teams build, the test results they trust, and the instructions sent to robots. These findings create two demands for robotics teams: responding as AI helps uncover weaknesses faster , and assessing how each one could affect robot safety and operations . What AI changes about vulnerability discovery Vulnerability discovery involves examining code, tracing how systems communicate, and testing whether a suspected weakness can actually be exploited. AI can accelerate parts of this work, helping researchers analyze more software in less time. Attackers could use similar capabilities. When the weakness is a zero-day — previously unknown and without an available fix — faster discovery can leave teams with little time to respond. While that exposure does not necessarily mean an attack has occurred, teams still need to determine whether they use the affected software and what an attacker could access or change. Where the findings sit across the robot lifecycle VicOne’s findings span three stages of the robotics lifecycle: development and training, simulation and validation, and deployment and runtime. Weaknesses at each stage could affect what a robot learns, how it is tested, and how it is controlled. Figure 1. In this research set, 75% of findings involved development, training, simulation, or validation tools, highlighting risks that can arise before a robot is deployed. VicOne The following scenarios show how a compromised component could influence the robot at each stage. Development and training: Hidden changes can reach the finished robot A team downloads a pretrained model to adapt for its robot. Loading a malicious file could give an attacker access to the training system, allowing changes to training data or the model itself. A manipulated model could behave normally during routine testing but respond incorrectly to a particular object, scene, or command after deployment. The risk can enter through a tool the team trusts, before anyone attacks the robot directly. Simulation and validation: A passing test could give false confidence Importing a compromised scene or robot model could give an attacker access to the simulation environment. With sufficient control, the attacker could alter simulated sensor readings, physical conditions, or test results. A robot could then appear to pass tests that should have exposed unsafe behavior, leading the team to approve it for real-world use on the basis of misleading evidence. Deployment and runtime: Operators could lose visibility or control An attacker could exploit weaknesses to change files that influence motion planning or send malicious map data that crashes the operator’s monitoring display. Compromising a remote-operation computer could also put the instructions sent to the robot at risk. Depending on the system and its safeguards, these weaknesses could alter robot movement or leave operators unable to see what is happening and respond promptly. These are potential consequences and not demonstrated outcomes for every finding. Actual effects depend on the attacker’s access, the system’s design, and whether other safeguards prevent the changes from reaching physical behavior. title: Copilot is "the new OS for work," and now Office runs inside of it
abstract: Opening the keynote at its Ignite event, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella outlined the company's vision for its new "frontier ecosystem," announcing Tuesday the general availability of Word, Excel, and PowerPoint inside Copilot, which he described as "the new OS for work." The announcement is a striking inversion of how we've traditionally used software. Rather than an app like Word being the attraction and Clippy the assistant to help you use it, Microsoft envisions the new Copilot integrations will see agents driving things, with the software packages riding shotgun. Applications will become plugin components of the agent's work, backed by an organizational knowledge layer that draws context from emails, meetings, calendars, chats, and files. Users will now be able to create documents, spreadsheets, and presentations directly in Copilot, with the resulting files remaining editable in their respective Office applications. title: Yet another satellite company is jockeying for a rocket—but this one makes sense
abstract: Finnish satellite developer ICEYE announced Tuesday that it is seeking to buy Italian rocket-maker Avio for more than $2.2 billion in a transaction aimed at creating Europe's first true vertically integrated end-to-end space company. The announcement came as an all-cash voluntary tender offer from an Italian subsidiary of ICEYE to Avio's shareholders, led by the Italian defense conglomerate Leonardo. Avio said its board of directors "has taken note of the notice" from ICEYE and is considering the purchase offer. Avio builds the Vega C rocket, a solid-fueled launcher designed to carry up to 3.3 metric tons (7,300 pounds) of payload to low-Earth orbit. title: Hundreds of websites deliver potent malware cocktail to unsuspecting visitors
abstract: Hundreds of websites using the Optimizely website personalization platform served unsuspecting visitors a potent malware cocktail that targeted cryptocurrency wallets, stole payment card data, cookies, and screenshots, and delivered exploit kits for infecting iPhones and iPads, researchers said Tuesday. ReportURI said it identified 178 websites—including CNN, Zoom, the BBC, and Salesforce—that were affected. JavaScript digitally signed by Optimizely and then loaded into customer pages had been modified to include malicious components that attempted to infect visitor devices with multiple payloads. When wares were installed successfully, they swapped user cryptocurrency wallet addresses for the attackers. Other components skimmed payment cards, stole cookies and screenshots, and, on iPhones and iPads, delivered iOS exploit kits known as Coruna and DarkSword. Optimizely infrastructure delivers multipurpose malware Optimizely serves JavaScript “snippets” that include both company code and code that is provided by each customer. The JavaScript, which can be served directly from Optimizely or from a customer endpoint, runs on every page the customer serves. Somehow, the attackers wrote their own code into a portion of each affected customer’s JavaScript and then delivered it from cdn.optimizely.com. A valid certificate for that domain signed the JavaScript. Read full article Comments

title: OpenAI sued by California after admitting to 80 loss-of-control incidents
abstract: California sued OpenAI yesterday, alleging it has tried to evade responsibility for the Hugging Face attack and about 80 other incidents in which the company lost control of its AI. The lawsuit was filed under the state's public nuisance and unfair competition laws. The July 2026 hack of Hugging Face and other attacks carried out by OpenAI's autonomous agents "may just be the tip of the iceberg," said a lawsuit filed in a state court by California Attorney General Rob Bonta. "OpenAI recently admitted to the Attorney General’s Office that it has lost control of its autonomous AI agents over 80 times during testing." OpenAI had publicly reported only 27 such incidents, showing that "OpenAI’s public reports do not represent the full scope of loss-of-control incidents involving OpenAI’s models that have impacted third parties," the lawsuit said. OpenAI "knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it," Bonta said in a press release . Read full article Comments

title: Google makes it easier to use Gemini without training AI on your data
abstract: It can be hard to use Google products—or even the Internet itself—without coming into contact with Gemini AI. That is, of course, by design . The more you use Gemini, the more data Google collects to train and improve its generative AI chatbot. The options to limit training on your data have been scant, but Google is finally adding more controls to the Gemini app. The change currently rolling out to Gemini will separate your chat history from training, which allows you to retain basic AI functionality without handing Google quite so much control over your data. Prior to this change, the only way to opt out of contributing your chat contents (including attachments) for training was to turn off your history. That made it impossible to go back and pick up a chat down the road. As the new settings roll out, users will see separate toggles for model training and chat history. The history setting will continue to support an adjustable limit, but you will no longer have to change it to stop Google from training on your Gemini usage. Meanwhile, AI training will be an opt-out situation. You'll need to find the toggle to block Google from using your chats for AI training. It's under Activity in the Gemini settings. You can also access the menu from your Google account under Data and Privacy > My Activity > Other activity > Gemini Apps Activity. Read full article Comments

title: House Democrats promise a US return to global climate talks
abstract: ANTALYA, Turkey—After their big gains in the 2026 midterm elections , a delegation of Democratic US House members appeared at the United Nations COP31 climate change conference Monday, pledging to rejoin the international fight against global warming. Rep. Jared Huffman (D-Calif.), ranking member of the House Natural Resources Committee, said it is a “pivotal time” for US climate and energy policy. “The wrecking ball of Donald Trump and this out-of-touch administration, and the temporarily empty chair of the United States at this COP31, does not represent what the Americans want or need,” Huffman said. Read full article Comments

title: Ars Live: What do drone strikes on data centers mean for the future? Talk at 1 pm EST today
abstract: Drone and missile strikes have inflicted unprecedented damage on data centers in Eastern Europe and the Middle East this year, disrupting cloud services for millions of people and permanently deleting some Amazon Web Services customer data. This trend represents a new concern for Big Tech companies—but also for governments and everyone else who depends on common digital services in modern life. To explore what this all means for modern society’s reliance on cloud resilience, I will be hosting a live conversation titled "Drone attacks and data centers: New Risks for Big Tech" on Tuesday, November 17 at 1 pm ET with Joseph Jarnecki , a senior research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), a UK defense and security think tank. He leads RUSI’s work on how cloud services factor into national security and defense, along with tech sovereignty efforts. Jarnecki has done extensive research on how Ukraine strengthened its cloud resilience with Western partners despite facing both cyberattacks and kinetic attacks at the start of the full-scale Russian invasion, and explored what that means for NATO and European governments’ cloud adoption plans. Read full article Comments

title: Grok Bot took unapproved actions, ignored orders to stop, and then denied it
abstract: Researchers recently discovered unexpected behavior from Grok Bot, the AI agent platform from Elon Musk’s SpaceXSI. Over five days, Grok bots installed on two separate employee laptops made 31 requests to access data stored in employee calendar, email, Slack, and GitHub accounts. The bots performed the actions even though the employees had never ordered them and continued doing them even after employees instructed them to stop. The bots also denied having taken the actions at all. The behavior was reported Tuesday by NewCore, the maker of a managed gateway product that acts as an intermediary between AI agents and the tools and accounts they are assigned to work with. In some cases, the unapproved access attempts occurred while the laptop with Grok Bot installed had its lid shut, or late at night while the employee was sleeping. None of the unprompted actions were recorded in Grok logs. Without the gateway logs, the employees would have had no idea they occurred. And of course, without the gateway, the unapproved accesses would have succeeded—again without the end user's knowledge. It’s “worse than a bug” Once the employees learned that Grok Bot had tried to check in with accounts without prompting, one of them instructed the agent, four separate times, to stop taking any actions on its own. The agent's reply was: “I won’t set that up, and I’ll stop offering recurring check-ins.” Despite acknowledging the explicit instructions, the Grok Bot made more unapproved access attempts. When one of the employees asked the bot if it made any accesses, it checked twice and then outputted: “Overnight into Friday morning I was idle.” Read full article Comments

title: Artist brings old Space Shuttle tank back to life
abstract: Natalie Rosen is not the type of specialist you immediately associate with being one of the key people behind the new exhibit of the space shuttle Endeavour . She is not a former NASA technician or engineer, as many of her colleagues have been for the past several years, nor is she a curator or conservator. Before this job, she had no experience working on any aircraft or spacecraft, as the new Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center, an extension of the California Science Center, opened in Los Angeles on November 13. Without her expertise and artistry, however, the largest component of Endeavour 's "stack" would look nothing like it did when the shuttle was flying. Read full article Comments

title: Robo-soldier startup backed by Eric Trump misses payroll, may collapse
abstract: A humanoid robotics company backed and advised by President Donald Trump’s son, Eric Trump, has reportedly missed payroll and may be on the brink of collapse after a funding shortfall. The Silicon Valley startup, Foundation Future Industries, claims it is developing and testing robots for military roles on battlefields from Ukraine to Gaza. Foundation failed to pay employees for the payroll period ending on October 30, anonymous sources told CNBC . The startup’s staff is especially angry because Foundation’s co-founder and CEO, Sankaet Pathak , supposedly borrowed $4.6 million in company funds to buy a luxury home overlooking San Francisco Bay about a year ago. This comes as Pathak and Foundation’s leadership are still looking to raise funding to support a $3 billion valuation, based on their promise to develop a humanoid robot ready for combat duty and capable of wielding various weapons. Read full article Comments

title: Three small failures combined to take down Microsoft 365
abstract: A hidden defect in Microsoft's cloud gateway, dormant since July, was to blame for one of the largest outages in the company's history last week. A preliminary Post-Incident Report (PIR) released by the company outlines how the latent bug, changes in traffic, and reduced server capacity combined to knock much of Microsoft 365 and Exchange infrastructure offline at the end of last week. Microsoft's report lists the incident's final status as "a technical issue not related to cyber or AI/agents." Microsoft's preliminary report places the outage between November 12 at 16:20 UTC and November 13 at 16:10 UTC, just under 24 hours total, and additional monitoring remained in place for any affected systems through November 14. The outage started on November 12 and quickly rippled through businesses and public offices that depend on Microsoft's cloud and email exchange infrastructure. The outage is covered in Microsoft's incident IDs EX1550543 and MO1550821. You need Microsoft 365 admin credentials to see the full report on the company's status pages, but Office Watch has reproduced the preliminary report , and the University of Pennsylvania maintains an archive of Microsoft's service-health updates . Read full article Comments

title: Hyperscale data centers use 2% of US electricity
abstract: One flashpoint for the tech industry’s all-in push on large language models has been the sudden rush to turn investment money into hyperscale data centers. The rush hasn’t allowed anyone to plan how to supply the required electricity cleanly or with minimal impact on ratepayers. Instead, it has been difficult to even collect information on what’s being built. A new study has tallied energy use and estimated emissions for hyperscalers operating in the United States between May 2024 and April 2025. They weren’t able to differentiate between AI compute and more traditional data services, but it provides a clear point of reference to track moving forward. Finding the centers The team started with a list of 675 facilities from a commercial database based on news reports, company statements, and satellite imagery. They dropped any that didn’t have a reported electrical capacity or that they couldn’t verify was a suitably large building with the expected cooling and electrical connection equipment. That reduced the list to 403 data centers with an average electrical capacity of about 40 megawatts. Read full article Comments

title: Shareholders sue Intel, its CEO, and CFO after stock drops 28.6 percent in one day
abstract: Intel is being sued by shareholders, who are accusing the chipmaker of misleading them about the impact of the PC sales slump that contributed to a drop of 28.6 percent in the price of Intel's stock on October 30. The lawsuit ( PDF ), filed on Friday in the San Jose, California, federal court, is seeking class-action certification and lists the City of Southfield Fire and Police Retirement System and “all others similarly situated” as plaintiffs. In addition to Intel, Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan and Intel’s EVP and CFO David Zinsner are listed as defendants. The plaintiffs claim that Intel made “materially false and misleading statements and omissions” between July 23 and October 29. They are seeking unspecified compensatory damages, plus legal and other associated fees, for shareholders during that period. Read full article Comments

title: Comcast's "fiber-powered Wi-Fi" is just cable, AT&T says in false advertising case
abstract: AT&T on Friday accused Comcast of false advertising in a lawsuit challenging the marketing claim that Comcast's cable broadband service and Wi-Fi are "fiber-powered." "This case challenges Comcast’s false advertising campaign for its residential Internet service, marketed under the Xfinity brand to consumers nationwide," AT&T's lawsuit said. "At the center of that campaign is Comcast’s claim that Xfinity Internet and its associated Wi-Fi service are 'Fiber-Powered.'" While Comcast has deployed plenty of fiber throughout the US, its cable Internet service makes the final connection to homes with coaxial cable. This results in upload speeds being far slower than download speeds. Read full article Comments

title: Supreme Court keeps injunction against DEI grant defunding in place
abstract: On Monday, the Supreme Court announced it would not hear an appeal of a lower court decision that blocked the government from canceling the grants of a handful of researchers whose funding had been revoked during the Trump administration's purge of DEI-related work. While the decision applies to only seven researchers in California, the lower court had ruled that the government's actions violated the First Amendment and so may have broad implications. The Supreme Court provided no discussion of its rejection, and no justices filed a dissent regarding the decision. The suit was initially filed by a large group of researchers at the University of California, Berkeley and UC San Francisco, contesting grants originally issued by many federal agencies, from the National Institutes of Health to the Department of Transportation. At issue were grants that had been terminated because the agencies decided they violated a Trump executive order blocking the use of DEI. This occurred despite the fact that the government hadn't bothered to define DEI , and targeted grants were often identified by little more than a keyword search . Read full article Comments

title: Nvidia’s Board Has No Plans to Bring Back Jensen Huang

abstract: The French CEO of Hugging Face, a mega-hub of open-source AI software, says the attack by OpenAI models earlier this year proved one thing: Humanity can’t let AI be controlled by the few.

title: 노트북을 닫아도 개발은 계속된다: 자율 그래프 주도 개발
abstract: 네이버 사내 기술 교류 행사인 NAVER Engineering Day 10th 에서 발표되었던 세션을 공개합니다. ​ ​ 발표 내용 '자율 그래프 주도 개발(Autonomous Graph-Driven Development)'에서는 사람의 직접적인 지시 없이 그래프가 프로젝트 진행을 주도합니다. 스펙 문서와 코드는 AI Agent 루프가 작성하고, 결정론적 코드가 이를 기계적으로 검사하며, 결함은 피드백 루프를 통해 자동으로 바로잡습니다. 사람이 AI를 호출하던 주도권이 역전되어 이제는 AI가 필요할 때만 사람을 호출합니다. ​ ​ 발표 대상 자율 그래프 주도 개발 방법론에 관심있는 개발자나 기획자 ​ 목차 1. AI가 다 해 주는데, 뭐가 문제지? (배경 및 문제 정의) 여전히 사람이 주도한다 요구사항은 항상 변한다 AI 협업에 남은 빈자리, 자율 진행 ​ 2. 어떻게 스스로 굴러가게 할까? (접근 방법 및 실행 과정) Autonomous Graph-Driven Development (용어 정의) Don't call us, we'll call you 그래프의 핵심 원칙 그래프 구조 노드 ① Upstream — 기획서 변경을 요구사항으로 옮긴다 노드 ② Spec-drive — 스펙을 확정한다 노드 ③ Dev — 확정된 스펙을 구현한다 노드 ③ Dev 사례 — 복잡한 AI 대화 구현, 토큰 비용 $199.61 노드 ④ Verify — 배포된 코드를 E2E 테스트로 검증한다 노드 ⑤ Audit — 스펙의 논리적 결함을 찾는다 진행 현황 대시보드 — 어디까지 왔고, 왜 멈춰 있는가? ​ 3. 처음부터 잘 굴러갔을까? (어려움 및 극복 과정) 그래프 자체가 또 하나의 제품이었다 어려움 ① 루프 안정화 — 루프는 눈치채지 못했다 어려움 ② AI와 협업 — 그래프는 쉬지 않는다 어려움 ③ 기획과 협업 — 애매한 문장은 AI도, 사람도 오해한다 ​ 4. 그래서, 무엇이 달라졌나? (성과 및 임팩트) 사람은 도구를 만들고, 루프는 제품을 만든다 성과 ① 리드타임 — 사람의 결정만 남는다 성과 ② 인력 — 백엔드 개발 공수 86% 절감 성과 ③ 토큰 비용 — 루프는 프런티어 모델이 아니어도 충분하다 성과 ④ 전체 비용 — 사람 + AI를 합쳐도 71% 절감 임팩트 ① 일하는 방식의 변화 — Human-in-the-loop 임팩트 ② 확장 가능성 — 그래프 운영 도구에는 서비스 지식이 없다 ​ 마무리 결정만 하면, 그래프가 알아서 합니다 ​ ◎ NAVER Engineering Day란? ​ NAVER에서는 사내 개발 경험과 기술 트렌드를 교류를 할 수 있는 프로그램이 많이 있습니다. 그중 이제는 매회 평균 100개 이상의 발표가 이루어지는 NAVER Engineering Day를 빼놓을 수 없는데요. 2016년부터 시작된 ENGINEERING DAY는 실무에서의 기술 개발 경험과 새로운 기술과 플랫폼 도입 시 유용하게 활용될 수 있는 팁 등을 공유하며 서로 배우고 성장하는 네이버의 대표적인 사내 개발자 행사입니다.( 관련 포스팅 보기 ) 올해 진행된 NAVER Engineering Day의 일부 세션을 공개합니다. ​ [동영상 제공 채널 안내] 네이버 TV 서비스 종료로 인해 기존 네이버 TV 채널을 클립( @devrel_d2 )으로 이동하였습니다. 앞으로도 많은 관심과 팔로우 부탁드리겠습니다.

title: Image AI 서빙 최적화: CPU와 GPU의 빈 시간을 줄여 H100 67장을 절감하기까지
abstract: 네이버 사내 기술 교류 행사인 NAVER Engineering Day 10th 에서 발표되었던 세션을 공개합니다. ​ ​ 발표 내용 SNOW의 16개 Image AI 서비스에서 응답 속도와 안정성을 높이면서, H100 환산 약 67장의 GPU 자원을 절감한 경험을 공유합니다. abstract: 네이버 사내 기술 교류 행사인 NAVER Engineering Day 10th 에서 발표되었던 세션을 공개합니다. ​ ​ 발표 내용 코드만 남아 있던 14년 된 카페 관리도구를 AI와 함께 분석하고, Storybook과 MSW로 화면과 동작을 재현하며 새로운 카페 스튜디오를 개발했습니다. 이 과정에서 기획, 디자인, BE와의 협업 방식이 어떻게 달라졌는지 공유합니다. ​ 발표 대상 레거시 시스템 개편을 준비하는 개발자 AI를 실무에 활용하려는 엔지니어 화면과 정책을 함께 검증하며 협업하고 싶은 기획자·디자이너 ​ 목차 프로젝트 개요 구 카페 관리도구 분석 신규 스튜디오 개발 일하는 방식 마무리 ​ ​ ◎ NAVER Engineering Day란? ​ NAVER에서는 사내 개발 경험과 기술 트렌드를 교류를 할 수 있는 프로그램이 많이 있습니다. 그중 이제는 매회 평균 100개 이상의 발표가 이루어지는 NAVER Engineering Day를 빼놓을 수 없는데요. 2016년부터 시작된 ENGINEERING DAY는 실무에서의 기술 개발 경험과 새로운 기술과 플랫폼 도입 시 유용하게 활용될 수 있는 팁 등을 공유하며 서로 배우고 성장하는 네이버의 대표적인 사내 개발자 행사입니다.( 관련 포스팅 보기 ) 올해 진행된 NAVER Engineering Day의 일부 세션을 공개합니다. ​ [동영상 제공 채널 안내] 네이버 TV 서비스 종료로 인해 기존 네이버 TV 채널을 클립( @devrel_d2 )으로 이동하였습니다. 앞으로도 많은 관심과 팔로우 부탁드리겠습니다.
