title: 지표 뒤에 숨은 맥락을 한눈에: New20 Timeline Hub 만들기
abstract: 대시보드에서 지표가 갑자기 움직인 날을 발견하면, 분석가는 자연스럽게 이유를 찾기 시작합니다. 그런데 숫자를 파고들기 전에 먼저 답해야 하는 질문이 있어요. “그날 제품에서 무슨 일이 있었을까요?” 새로운 화면이 배포됐을 수도 있고, 대상 유저 조건이 바뀌었을 수도 있습니다. 실험이 시작됐거나 혜택 정책이 달라졌을 수도 있죠. 이 기록들은 대개 어딘가에 남아 있지만, 한곳에 모여 있지는 않습니다. 배포 채널을 검색하고, 관련 PR을 찾아보고, 정책 문서와 논의 이력을 비교해야 비로소 당시의 상황을 그릴 수 있어요. 이 글에서는 페이스페이 프로모션 New20의 맥락을 한눈에 살펴보기 위해 만든 New20 Timeline Hub 를 소개합니다. 흩어진 기록을 어떻게 하나의 시간축으로 연결했는지, 자동으로 모은 정보를 어떤 기준으로 정리했는지, 그리고 신뢰할 수 있는 맥락을 만들기 위해 무엇을 고민했는지 이야기해 보겠습니다. 질문은 반복되는데, 답은 흩어져 있었습니다 New20은 참여한 유저가 일정 기간 페이스페이로 결제할 때 혜택을 제공하는 프로모션입니다. 반복 결제를 유도하는 것이 목표인 만큼, 혜택 정책뿐 아니라 참여 대상, 유저가 만나는 화면, 노출 지면, 실험이 계속 바뀝니다. 이런 제품을 분석하다 보면 비슷한 질문을 자주 받습니다. “9월 둘째 주에 참여가 왜 튀었나요?” ”지금 NAU 대상 조건이 정확히 어떤건가요?” ”이 경로로 들어오면 어떤 화면이 뜨나요?” ”그 때 쿠폰은 얼마였죠?” 답을 찾는 데 필요한 자료는 회의록 , GitHub PR, 정책 문서, 디자인 보드, 세그먼트 정의, 대시보드에 나뉘어 있었습니다. 관련 자료가 없어서가 아니라 기록을 이어 붙이는 비용 이 문제였어요. 각 자료는 자기 목적에는 충실했지만, 분석가가 특정 시점의 제품 상태를 복원하기에는 조각이 흩어져 있었습니다. 예를 들어 지표가 오른 시점에 배포가 있었다는 사실만 알아서는 충분하지 않습니다. 어떤 유저를 대상으로 했는지, 어떤 화면에서 노출됐는지, 같은 기간 다른 실험은 없었는지도 함께 살펴봐야 합니다. 게다가 변경 시점이 가깝다는 사실만으로 지표 변화의 원인을 확정할 수는 없습니다. 맥락은 인과관계의 답이라기보다, 어떤 가설을 검증해야 할지 찾는 출발점 에 가깝습니다. 힌트는 하나의 시간축에 있었습니다 허브를 만들 때 참고한 것은 Meta의 Timeline 형식 내부 도구 를 커머스 도메인의 배포 조회 도구에 적용한 사례였습니다. 커머스 사례에서는 팀과 서비스별로 한 줄씩 두고, 배포를 점으로 표시한 뒤 변경 유형을 색으로 구분했어요. 여러 변경을 같은 시간축에서 볼 수 있다는 점이 인상적이었습니다. 저는 이 방식을 분석가의 질문에 맞게 가져왔습니다. 배포만 나열하는 대신 제품 맥락을 다섯 가지 갈래로 나눴어요. 정책·혜택: 어떤 혜택과 운영 정책이 바뀌었는지 세그먼트: 누구에게 적용되는지, 대상 조건이 어떻게 달라졌는지 노출 지면: 유저가 어디에서 어떤 화면과 메시지를 만나는지 실험: 무엇을 검증하기 위해 어떤 시도를 했는지 데이터·대시보드: 분석과 모니터링에 필요한 데이터가 어떻게 연결되는지 이렇게 나누면 날짜는 하나로 유지하면서도 질문에 따라 필요한 갈래를 살펴볼 수 있습니다. 예를 들어 참여 지표를 이해하려면 정책 변경뿐 아니라 같은 시기의 노출 지면과 실험도 함께 확인할 수 있어요. 타임라인의 점에는 상태도 표시했습니다. 채운 점은 PR이나 배포를 통해 개발 반영이 확인된 변경 , 빈 점은 논의 기록은 있지만 개발 반영이 확인되지 않은 항목 입니다. 논의된 내용과 실제 반영된 내용을 같은 확실성으로 읽지 않도록 하기 위해서예요. 여러 기록을 하나의 ‘변경’으로 묶기 타임라인을 만들 때 부딪힌 문제는 관련 링크를 날짜순으로 늘어놓는 것만으로는 제품의 변화를 이해하기 어렵다는 점이었습니다. 하나의 제품 변경이 서버와 프론트엔드 PR, 데이터 작업, 배포 요약, 운영 논의 등의 여러 채널에 각각 기록되기 때문입니다. 예를 들어 9월 8일로 정리된 ‘현장참여 사후적립 출시’ 항목에는 PR 9건과 회의록 5건, 총 14개의 근거가 연결돼 있습니다. 이 변경에는 매장에서 먼저 결제한 유저가 이후 New20에 참여했을 때 적립을 사후에 지급하는 내용과 함께 안내·알림 퍼널, 인앱 진입점 관련 변경, 미수령 세그먼트 뷰가 연결돼 있었어요. 일부 서버·프론트엔드 반영과 관련 후속 작업은 서로 다른 날짜에 걸쳐 있었습니다. 이 기록들을 각각 별도의 점으로만 보여주면 실제로는 하나의 흐름인 일이 여러 사건처럼 보일 수 있습니다. 반대로 하나로 묶기만 하고 원문을 남기지 않으면, 요약이 무엇을 근거로 하는지 확인하기 어렵습니다. 그래서 허브에서는 변경을 읽기 쉬운 단위로 묶되, 그 판단에 사용한 원문을 함께 연결 했습니다. 이 방식의 핵심은 요약을 정답으로 만드는 데 있지 않습니다. 필요한 사람이 변경의 개요를 빠르게 파악하고, 중요한 판단을 할 때는 원문으로 돌아가 확인할 수 있게 하는 데 있습니다. 시간순 목록을 넘어, 질문별로 찾아보기 같은 자료라도 질문에 따라 필요한 출발점은 다릅니다. 그래서 허브에는 시간축 외에도 제품 맥락을 다른 관점에서 볼 수 있는 화면을 두었습니다. 히스토리: 날짜별 변경과 연결된 근거를 확인합니다. 노출 현황: 진입 경로와 유저 상태에 따라 어떤 화면이 보이는지 살펴봅니다. 세그먼트: 현재 대상 조건과 과거 변경 이력을 함께 봅니다. 관계 보기: 같은 주제에 속한 결정, 화면, 문서를 연결해서 탐색합니다. 쿠폰 발급 종료: 지면별 종료 현황을 확인합니다. 데이터: 대시보드, 리포트, 정책 문서로 이동합니다. 출처·범위: 어떤 자료를 모았고 어디에 빈틈이 있는지 확인합니다. 예전에는 “현재 대상 조건이 뭐죠?”라는 질문에 답하려면 SQL과 문서, 변경 스레드를 각각 찾아 맞춰 봐야 했습니다. 허브에서는 세그먼트 화면에서 현재 조건과 변경 이력을 함께 살펴볼 수 있습니다. “그날 무슨 일이 있었죠?”라는 질문은 히스토리에서 날짜를 좁힌 뒤 관련 원문으로 이동하는 방식으로 풀 수 있고요. 중요한 것은 모든 정보를 한 화면에 복사하는 것이 아니라, 질문에서 근거까지 이어지는 경로를 짧게 만드는 것 이었습니다. 매일 쌓이는 맥락을 정리하는 방법 허브가 한 번 만든 뒤 멈춘 문서가 되지 않도록, 매일 아침 기록을 수집하고 정리하는 과정을 붙였습니다. 1. 기록이 있는 곳에서 모읍니다 배포 요약 채널, 여러 저장소의 PR, 문서 목록, 결정 노트 등 자동으로 가져올 수 있는 자료부터 모았습니다. PR은 서버가 매시간 별도로 가져오고, 다른 자료는 아침 스크립트로 정리합니다. 아침 스크립트 실행에는 약 5~10분이 걸립니다. 모든 소스를 한꺼번에 완벽하게 연결하기보다, 먼저 기존에 기록이 쌓이고 있는 곳을 파악하는 것이 출발점이었어요. 2. 기록된 날짜와 실제 맥락의 날짜를 구분합니다 자동 수집에서 가장 어려운 문제 중 하나는 날짜였습니다. 어떤 결정이 나중에 지식 노트에 적재되면, 적재일을 사건의 날짜로 착각하기 쉽습니다. 하지만 분석가에게 필요한 것은 대개 노트가 저장된 날이 아니라, 결정이나 변경이 실제로 일어난 시점 입니다. 예를 들어 5월 15일에 논의한 내용이 9월 30일에 지식 노트로 적재된 경우가 있었습니다. 허브에서는 노트의 적재일을 그대로 쓰지 않고 근거가 되는 논의 시점을 확인해 날짜를 바로잡았습니다. 그렇지 않았다면 수개월이 지난 뒤의 지표 변화와 과거 논의가 잘못 나란히 놓일 수 있었겠죠. 3. 갈래와 상태를 붙이고, 표현을 정리합니다 수집한 항목은 정책·혜택, 세그먼트, 노출 지면, 실험, 데이터·대시보드 중 적절한 갈래로 나눕니다. 개발 반영이 확인됐는지, 논의만 확인됐는지도 구분합니다. 읽는 사람을 위해 표현도 정리했습니다. 이름을 가리고, 내부에서 쓰는 ‘편입’ 같은 단어는 맥락에 맞게 ‘참여’로 통일했어요. 기록을 모으는 일과 다른 사람이 이해할 수 있도록 맥락을 번역하는 일은 별개의 작업이었습니다. 4. 요약 옆에 원문을 남깁니다 각 항목에는 확인 가능한 PR, 회의록, 지식 노트 링크를 연결했습니다. 자동으로 만든 요약이나 수작업으로 정리한 문장 모두 틀릴 수 있기 때문입니다. 특히 정

title: 판단에만 집중하세요: 토스 타겟팅 모델 개발 자동화
abstract: 불과 2년 전만 해도 모델을 하나 만들려면 내부망에서 Jupyter 노트북을 켜고, 쿼리를 짜고, 수많은 함수를 직접 만들어야 했어요. 그런데 저희는 ML Engineer(MLE)가 반복적이고 번거로운 일보다는, 현재 일의 성과를 더 개선하기 위한 점을 찾고 임팩트를 줄 일에 집중하는데 더 많은 시간을 써야 한다고 생각했습니다. 그래서 고객 타겟팅 모델 개발 프레임워크 TASTE 를 꾸준히 가다듬어 모델 학습 시간을 2주에서 1일로 줄였어요. 그러나 모델 사용처로부터 받는, 그리고 모델을 개발한 MLE 스스로 묻는 "이 모델을 써도 되나?"라는 질문에 답하기 위한 판단 과정에서 늘 필요한 모델 비교와 평가 및 모니터링은 여전히 손으로 해야 했어요. 저희는 그 과정을 TASTE의 파이프라인에 더했어요. 이 글에서는 MLE 가 모델 하나를 쓰기까지 거치는 비교 네 가지를 차례로 따라가며, 각각을 어떻게 자동화했는지 소개합니다. 모델 하나를 쓰기까지 네 번 비교해요 TASTE 에서는 설정 파일 하나로 후보 피쳐 수집 → 피쳐 선정 → 학습 → 추론·적재 → 평가가 하나의 파이프라인으로 돌아요. 그런데 이 파이프라인이 내놓은 모델을 쓸지 판단하기 위해 다음 네 가지 질문에 답해야 했고, 이를 위한 계산을 사람이 따로 해야 했습니다. 질문 무엇과 무엇을 비교하나 예전 지금 1️⃣ 피쳐를 몇 개 쓸까 피쳐 수 K 끼리 MLE 가 경험으로 비율을 정함 auto_k 가 K 별 성능을 재서 고름 2️⃣ 어떤 구조를 쓸까 트리와 딥러닝 단계별 트리 여러 개를 곱한 조합을 손으로 비교 같은 평가셋으로 나란히 재서 고름 3️⃣ 기존 모델보다 나은가 새 모델과 기존 모델 점수와 정답을 손으로 조인 학습이 끝나면 평가 보고서가 나옴 4️⃣ 입력 데이터를 믿어도 되나 날짜끼리 (학습 때와 오늘, 평가일 사이) 확인하지 않음 결손이 한도를 넘으면 적재를 멈추고, 평가는 여러 날짜에서 함 1️⃣ 피쳐를 몇 개 쓸까: auto_k 피쳐 선택 이후 남은 고민 모델 성능을 기준으로 사용할 피쳐 수를 자동으로 고르는 auto_k 알고리즘은 팀 채팅 스레드에서 시작했어요. 지금까지 피쳐 수는 MLE가 정한 비율로 정했어요. 후보 피쳐를 중요도 순으로 세운 뒤 상위 몇 %만 남기는 방식이에요. 이 방식은 데이터 개수나 예측 대상의 특성과 상관없이 같은 비율을 쓰기 때문에 학습 효율과 성능이 떨어질 수 있습니다. 도메인·데이터·모델마다 알맞은 비율이 달라, MLE가 경험만으로 ‘상위 몇 %’를 자신 있게 정하기도 어렵죠. 먼저 대안으로 떠올린 건 중요도가 급격히 떨어지는 지점(Elbow)에서 자르는 방법이었어요. 그러나 이 방법으로 피쳐 갯수를 자른 다음(ex. 20개) 모형 성능을 평가하면, 이보다 더 많은 피쳐 수(ex. 75개)를 포함한 모형의 성능 지표가 훨씬 높은 경우가 많이 발생했어요. 이는 중요도가 몇 개 피쳐에 크게 몰려 있어 중요도가 급히 떨어지는 점이 구조적으로 앞쪽에서 포착되는데, 그 점에서 자르고 나도 여전히 모형 성능 개선에 기여하는 피쳐는 남아있기 때문이었습니다. 피쳐 수 (K) AUROC PR-AUC 458개와 PR-AUC 차이 상위 5% 회수율 20 99.1% 77.4% 유의하게 낮음 91.5% 30 99.5% 74.2% 유의하게 낮음 93.5% 50 100.0% 88.7% 유의하게 낮음 99.4% 75 100.1% 98.4% 구별 안 됨 100.8% 100 100.2% 100.0% 구별 안 됨 101.2% 458 100% 100% 기준 100% 결국 중요도 곡선의 모양만 보고 사용 피쳐 수의 컷오프 점을 정하는 방식은 적절하지 않았던 것입니다. 필요한 건 ‘성능이 어디서 더 오르지 않는가’였고, 그건 성능을 직접 재야 알 수 있었어요. 그래서 검증에 쓴 절차를 그대로 자동화한 것이 auto_k 예요(자체 조어). 요약하면, 같은 모델 설정에서 피쳐 수를 늘려가며 성능을 측정하고, 성능 개선이 멈추는 지점에서 사용할 최적의 피쳐 수를 결정해 보자는 아이디어예요. 이 방법을 검증하기 위해 어떤 모델의 후보로 걸러진 피쳐 458개를 피쳐 중요도(Feature Importance) 순으로 줄여 가며 성능을 쟀어요. 위 표에서 458개와 통계적으로 구별되지 않는 가장 작은 개수는 75개였어요. 피쳐를 84% 줄여도 유의한 성능 손실이 없으면서, 모델의 훈련시간이나 메모리는 절감할 수 있었죠. 그래서 중요도로 순서를 정하고, 성능으로 개수를 정했어요. auto_k는 이렇게 동작해요 auto_k는 위 실험을 그대로 자동화한 기능입니다. 후보 피쳐 전체로 트리를 한 번 학습해 피쳐 중요도 순위를 매겨요. 샘플 데이터에 대해서, 사용할 피쳐의 수 K = 10, 20, 30, 50, 75, 100, 150 등 마다 상위 K개로 다시 학습하고, 가장 최근 기간의 평가셋에서 PR-AUC를 재요. 최고점과 통계적으로 구별되지 않는 K 중 가장 작은 값을 골라요. 앞 표에서는 75예요. 어떤 K 도 최고점과 구별되지 않으면 판단할 근거가 없다고 보고, 기존 비율 방식을 그대로 써요. 피쳐를 줄이고도 성능은 높아졌어요. 한 상품의 구매 전환을 고객별로 예측하는 모델은 모델 구조를 딥러닝에서 트리로 바꾸고 (실험 내용은 2️⃣절의 딥러닝 vs Tree 참조), auto_k로 피쳐를 고르자, 피쳐를 절반 넘게 줄이면서도 상위 5% 회수율이 고관여 세그먼트 대비 약 1.7배 올랐습니다. 또한 실제 마케팅 메시지 발송 실험에서도 성과가 이어졌어요. auto_k로 피쳐를 고른 또 다른 상품 모델의 점수 상위 1% 고객은 기존 규칙 기반 세그먼트보다 클릭률이 약 5배, 신청 전환율이 약 2.6배 높았어요. 연령 구성을 맞춰 비교해도 클릭률은 3배 이상, 신청 전환율은 2배 이상 높았어요. 2️⃣ 어떤 구조를 쓸까: 트리와 딥러닝을 나란히 재요 모델 구조를 고를 때도 같은 데이터·같은 평가셋에서 성능을 비교해요. 노출 → 진입 → 클릭 → 신청처럼 단계가 이어지는 퍼널 모델은 종래에는 단계마다 트리 모델을 따로 학습해 왔어요. 진입할 확률, 진입한 고객이 상품을 누를 확률, 누른 고객이 신청할 확률을 각각 학습한 뒤 추론이 끝나면 점수를 곱해 최종 점수를 만들었습니다. 운영도 해석도 쉬운 방식이지만 단계끼리 서로 남남이라는 한계가 있었습니다. 진입 단계 모델이 배운 신호가 클릭·신청 모델로 전달되지 않아요. 데이터가 가장 적은 마지막 단계(신청)일수록 앞 단계에서 쌓인 신호가 절실한데 그걸 쓰지 못했죠. 조합을 고르는 일에도 손이 많이 갔어요. 3단계 퍼널 하나에 모델을 최대 다섯 개 학습하고 점수를 곱하는 조합 열한 가지의 성능을 직접 비교했습니다. 채널(푸시·홈 화면·메시지)이 바뀌면 이 과정을 통째로 다시 했고, 퍼널이 수십 개다 보니 운영하는 트리 모델도 수십 개로 불어났어요. 그래서 지금은, 퍼널 전체를 한 모델로 학습하는 딥러닝 모델 AITM(Adaptive Information Transfer Multi-task, KDD 2021)을 TASTE 설정에서 고를 수 있게 구현했습니다. 이 모델이 우리의 최선이라고 믿는 것은 아니지만 앞으로도 확장성 높고 유연한 프레임워크 덕분에 다양한 모델의 형상을 추가할 수 있어요. 퍼널 모델 구조와 라벨 설계 퍼널 모델인 AITM 이 ‘추론한 뒤에 곱하기’와 갈라지는 지점은 두 장치입니다. 정보 전달 (Adaptive Information Transfer): 앞 단계에서 학습한 표현에 변환을 적용한 뒤, 현재 단계의 표현과 Attention 으로 결합해요. 앞 단계 정보를 얼마나 참고할지 고객마다 가중치로 정하는 셈이에요. 단조성 제약 (Label Constraint): 뒤 단계 확률이 앞 단계 확률보다 커지면 그 초과분만큼 손실에 벌점을 더해요. 아래 그림은 단계별 표현이 정보 전달 모듈을 거쳐 다음 단계로 넘어가는 AITM 의 구조예요. 이 모델을 쓰려고 파이프라인을 새로 짜지는 않습니다. title: 같은 모델, 다른 예측
abstract: 안녕하세요. 토스코어 Machine Learning Platform 팀 김준호, 송석현입니다. 추천 모델은 과거에 어떤 상품을 추천했고 사용자가 클릭하거나 구매했는지에 대한 기록에, 사용자와 상품의 피처를 연결해 학습해요. 이렇게 학습한 모델로 온라인에서 추천할 때는 요청이 들어온 시점에 온라인 저장소에서 제공하는 피처를 조회해 예측해요. 이 추천 기록은 이후 모델을 학습하는데 다시 사용돼요. 그런데 피처는 시간이 지나면서 달라지기 때문에, 학습 데이터를 만드는 시점의 값을 그대로 가져오면 실제 추천할 때와 다른 정보를 사용하게 돼요. 그래서 과거 시점에 맞는 피처를 연결하는 Point-in-Time (PIT) 조인을 사용해요. 같은 사용자나 상품의 피처 중에서, 학습 데이터에 지정한 기준 시각을 넘지 않는 가장 최근 값을 가져오는 방식이에요. 토스의 Trainkit에서 PIT 조인을 지원하는 방식은 이전 글 에서 소개했어요. 다만 피처에 기록된 시각과 실제 서빙에 반영된 시각이 항상 같지는 않아요. 배치로 생성한 피처를 온라인 저장소에 업로드하는데 시간이 걸리기 때문이에요. 따라서 배치 데이터의 기준 시각으로 피처를 선택하면, 요청 당시에는 아직 서빙되지 않았던 값을 학습에 사용할 수도 있어요. 이처럼 학습할 때와 실제 예측할 때 사용하는 피처에 차이가 생기는 현상을 Training-Serving Skew 라고 해요. 토스 추천 시스템에서도 학습과 서빙에서 서로 다른 파티션을 사용하거나, 업로드 중 피처 값과 파티션 정보가 어긋나는 문제를 겪었어요. 집계 대상에서 빠진 값이 온라인 저장소에 남아 계속 서빙되는 경우도 있었어요. 이 글에서는 세 가지 문제가 발생한 원인과, 이를 해결하기 위해 검토하고 적용한 방법을 소개해요. Problem 1 - 학습과 서빙에서 서로 다른 파티션 사용 추천 모델은 사용자의 행동 이력, 상품 정보, 사용자 정보 등 여러 피처를 함께 사용해요. 토스에서는 이러한 피처들을 테이블에 저장하고, 여러 테이블을 피처 서비스로 묶어서 조회해요. 하나의 모델에서 여러 피처 서비스를 사용하기도 해요. 각 피처 테이블은 배치로 데이터를 생성해요. 생성한 데이터는 기준 시각별 파티션으로 보관하고, 온라인 저장소에 업로드해 서빙에 사용해요. 예를 들어 매시간 생성하는 테이블이라면, 09시, 10시 파티션을 각각 보관하는 식이에요. 그런데 배치 데이터가 만들어진 시각과 실제로 서빙을 시작한 시각은 같지 않아요. 이는 온라인 저장소에 업로드하는 시간이 필요하고, 테이블마다 업로드가 끝나는 시점도 다르기 때문이에요. 10시 5분에 추천 요청이 들어왔다고 해볼게요. 이 때, 사용자 정보를 담고 있는 피처 테이블은 업로드가 완료되어 10시 파티션을 사용하지만, 상품 정보를 담고 있는 피처 테이블은 아직 업로드가 끝나지 않아 09시 파티션을 사용할 수 있어요. 같은 요청에서도 테이블마다 서로 다른 시점의 데이터를 사용하는 거예요. 이제 이 요청을 학습 데이터로 만드는 과정을 살펴볼게요. 기존에는 요청이 발생한 시각을 기준으로 피처 파티션을 선택했어요. 앞의 요청은 10시 5분에 발생했으므로, 사용자 정보와 상품 정보 모두 10시 파티션에서 가져오는거에요. 하지만 실제 추론에서는 상품 정보로 09시 파티션을 사용했어요. 결국 같은 요청에 대해 서빙에서는 09시 데이터를 학습에서는 10시 데이터 를 사용하게 되는거에요. 학습과 서빙이 동일한 파티션을 사용하게 하기 위해서 두 가지 방법을 검토했어요. 방법 1-1. 모든 추론 요청을 로그로 적재 가장 직관적인 방법은 모든 추론 요청에서 실제 사용한 피처를 로그로 적재하는 것이에요. 예를 들어 사용자 A에게 상품 X를 추천할 때 피처 값 5 를 사용했다면, 어떤 추천 요청에서 사용한 값인지 알 수 있도록 로그에 함께 남겨요. 이후 학습 데이터를 만들 때는 사용자가 상품 X를 클릭했는지에 대한 결과와 로그에 저장한 값 5 를 연결해요. 실제 예측에 사용한 값이 로그에 있으니, 원본 피처 테이블에서 당시의 값을 다시 조회할 필요가 없어요. 다만 모든 요청에서 사용한 피처 값을 로그로 남기려면 저장 비용을 고려해야 해요. 당시 규모로 계산했을 때 하루에도 수십 TB의 로그가 쌓일 것으로 예상했어요. 여기에 로그를 전송하는 비용과 학습 데이터를 만들 때 읽고 처리하는 비용도 더해져요. 토스에서는 여러 실험을 동시에 진행하고 있어, 각 실험에서 사용하는 피처 값을 모두 기록하면 비용 부담이 커져요. 그래서 피처 값 전체를 저장하는 대신, 더 적은 정보로 서빙 당시의 값을 다시 가져올 수 있는 방법을 검토했어요. 방법 1-2. 사용한 파티션을 기록 피처 값 전체를 로그로 남기는 대신, 실제 서빙에 사용한 피처의 파티션만 기록하는 방법도 있어요. 배치로 생성한 피처는 이미 기준 시각별 파티션으로 보관하고 있어서, 요청마다 사용한 파티션과 조회 대상을 정확히 남기면 학습에서도 같은 값을 다시 가져올 수 있어요. 예를 들어 10시 5분에 들어온 요청에서 상품 피처로 09시 파티션을 사용했다면, 해당 요청의 로그에 상품 피처는 09시 파티션에서 가져왔다는 정보를 남겨요. 이후 학습 데이터를 만들 때도 이 기록을 따라 09시 파티션에서 해당 상품의 피처를 가져와요. 요청이 발생한 시각으로 파티션을 추정하지 않고, 실제 서빙에 사용한 파티션을 선택하는 거예요. 이 방식으로 같은 값을 가져오려면 학습에 필요한 기간 동안 과거 파티션을 보관해야 해요. 또한 보관한 파티션의 값을 나중에 덮어쓰지 않는 것도 중요해요. 파티션을 정확히 기록했더라도 그 안의 값이 바뀌면, 실제 예측에 사용했던 피처를 재현할 수 없기 때문이에요. 우리는 이미 보관하고 있는 배치 데이터에서 피처 값을 가져오고, 요청 로그에는 사용한 파티션 정보만 남기는 방식을 선택했어요. 피처 값 전체를 요청마다 반복해서 저장하지 않아도 되기 때문에, 로그의 크기와 이를 전송하고 보관하는 비용을 줄일 수 있어요. Problem 2 - 피처 값과 파티션 정보가 서로 다른 시점에 갱신 09시 파티션 ( P09 ) 을 서빙하던 테이블에 10시 파티션( P10 )을 업로드한다고 해볼게요. 업로더는 서빙 중인 테이블에 새 피처 값을 행마다 덮어써요. 사용자 A의 행을 먼저 갱신하면, 그때부터 A를 조회하는 요청에는 P10 의 값이 반환돼요. 아직 갱신하지 않은 사용자 B를 조회하면 같은 시각에도 P09 의 값이 반환돼요. 그런데 요청 로그에 남기는 파티션 정보는 테이블마다 하나였어요. 여기에는 마지막으로 업로드를 마친 파티션을 기록하기 때문에, P10 파티션의 모든 데이터 업로드가 끝날 때 까지는 A를 조회해도 B를 조회해도 파티션 정보는 P09 로 남아요. 두 요청 모두 같은 파티션을 기록하지만, 먼저 갱신된 A의 경우에는 그 기록이 실제로 사용한 값과 어긋나요. 그림에서 10시 5분에 들어온 추천 요청은 사용자 A의 새 조회 횟수인 5를 사용했어요. 나중에 이 요청을 학습 데이터로 만들 때 로그에 남은 P09 에서 A의 조회 횟수를 가져오면, 학습에서는 이전 값인 3을 사용하게 돼요. 방법 2-1. 테이블 행마다 파티션을 저장하기 이 문제를 해결하는 방법 중 하나는 row마다 피처 값과 해당 값의 파티션을 함께 저장하는 것이에요. 예를 들어 업로드 중 어떤 row가 10시 데이터로 갱신됐다면, 그 row의 파티션 정보도 10시로 바꾸는 거예요. 그러면 업로드가 모두 끝나기 전에도 새 값을 서빙하면서, 해당 값이 어느 파티션에서 왔는지 정확히 기록할 수 있어요. 다만 이 방식을 적용하려면 업로더에서 row마다 파티션을 저장하고, 서빙에서는 조회한 row별 파티션을 로그로 남기며, 학습에서도 이 정보를 이용해 피처를 가져오도록 변경해야 해요. 우리는 이 구조를 한 번에 변경하기보다, 기존의 테이블 단위 파티션 정보를 활용해, 먼저 학습과 서빙의 차이를 줄이기로 했어요. 행별 기록을 도입하는 데 필요한 작업량에 비해 얼마나 효과가 있을지 확인되지 않은 상태였기 때문이에요. 테이블 단위의 파티션 정보를 계속 사용하려면, 업로드 중 먼저 갱신된 row가 바로 서빙되지 않도록 해야 해요. 그래서 다음으로 설명할 블루/그린 방식을 선택해, 서빙하는 데이터와 테이블

title: Closing the GitHub Actions Monitoring Gap: Observing ARC Runners with an Exporter
abstract: Hi, I’m Uno from the Delivery part of Karrot’s SRE team. Our team’s mission is to run Kontrol, our internal deployment platform on Kubernetes, and manage the company-wide CI system that mostly relies on GitHub Actions. In this post I’ll introduce the exporter we built to see which Jobs are waiting and which Runner is running each Job. I’ll also share how we improved it in production. A Workflow defines what happens when an event such as a push or pull request occurs. Each Workflow is split into Jobs such as test and build that run on execution environments called Runners. If no Runner is free, a Job waits until one becomes available. name: Simple # 1. Workflow: defines the automation on: workflow_dispatch: jobs: run_shell_command: # 2. Job: the unit that gets a Runner and runs name: Actions are amazing runs-on: arc-test-runner steps: # 3. Step: the commands the Job executes - name: Say hello run: | echo "Hello!" Runners can be GitHub-hosted or self-hosted. At Karrot we mainly use self-hosted Runners on our own Kubernetes clusters. These are managed by a Kubernetes operator called ARC (Actions Runner Controller) . ARC organizes Runners into groups called Runner Scale Sets and scales each set according to Job demand. Each set defines the Runner image and resources, along with minimum and maximum Runner counts. A Workflow can specify a Runner Scale Set in runs-on so its Jobs are assigned to Runners in that set. Source: https://docs.github.com/en/actions/concepts/runners/actions-runner-controller Even with autoscaling, Jobs don’t always start immediately. A GitHub outage or a spike in Job requests can leave them stuck in the Queued state. While operating ARC, we often heard developers say, “My Action is stuck in Queued and won’t run.” Answering that question wasn’t easy with the data we had. We often had to wait for an announcement on GitHub’s status page or infer the cause from ARC’s built-in metrics. ARC’s built-in metrics show aggregate counts of Runners and Jobs, but they don’t tell us how many Jobs are waiting for a Runner, how long they’ve been waiting, or which Runner Pod is running a given Job. With that information, we could give developers a better understanding of what was happening with their Jobs. While looking for a solution, we found an issue in the ARC repository proposing to add Job information to Runner Pods as labels. Adopting that approach would require controller changes and additional permissions, as well as a separate setup to collect the labels as metrics, so we decided to build our own solution. We built action-runner-job-exporter to connect Runner Pods to their Assigned Jobs and track Jobs still waiting for a Runner. There are three key components for the exporter, which are separate binaries. Collector associates Job names with Runner Pods, Webhook tracks waiting Jobs, and StateStore persists Webhook's state. action-runner-job-exporter architecture How ARC Runners work Before getting into the exporter, let’s look at how ARC creates a Runner Pod and how a Job reaches it. Each Runner Scale Set has a Listener Pod that keeps a session open with GitHub and waits for new Job assignments. A Workflow starts in a repository, and GitHub assigns each Job to the Runner Scale Set that matches its runs-on. The Listener works out how many Runners are needed from the assigned Jobs and the min/max Runner settings, then updates the replicas of the EphemeralRunnerSet. ARC creates that many EphemeralRunner resources, fetches a one-time registration config (JIT config) from GitHub for each, and starts the Runner Pods. Once a Runner Pod registers with GitHub, GitHub assigns a Job to it. After the Job starts, the Listener receives the assignment and writes the repository and Job details into the status field of that EphemeralRunner. The Runner process exits after the Job finishes and ARC cleans up the Runner’s resources. Runner creation and Job assignment ARC creates the Runners and GitHub decides which Job goes to each one. B

title: GitHub Actions 모니터링의 빈칸: Exporter로 ARC Runner 관측하기
abstract: 안녕하세요, 당근 SRE팀 딜리버리 파트에서 일하고 있는 Uno(우노)예요. 딜리버리 파트는 Kubernetes 환경 기반의 사내 배포 플랫폼 Kontrol을 운영하고 GitHub Actions 중심의 전사 CI 시스템을 관리해요. 이번 글에서는 GitHub Actions를 운영하며 Job의 대기 현황과 Job을 실행 중인 Runner를 파악하기 위해 exporter를 만들고 개선한 과정을 소개할게요. exporter를 소개하기에 앞서 GitHub Actions의 구조를 간단히 살펴볼게요. GitHub Actions에서는 push나 Pull Request 같은 이벤트가 발생했을 때 실행할 작업의 흐름을 Workflow로 정의해요. 하나의 Workflow는 테스트, 빌드처럼 여러 Job으로 나뉘어 각 Job은 Runner라는 실행 환경에 배정되어 실행되고 할당 가능한 Runner가 없으면 Job은 배정될 때까지 대기해요. name: Simple # 1. Workflow: 자동화 작업 정의 on: workflow_dispatch: jobs: run_shell_command: # 2. Job: Runner 배정 및 실행 단위 name: Actions are amazing runs-on: arc-test-runner steps: # 3. Step: 작업 실행 절차 및 명령 - name: Say hello run: | echo "Hello!" GitHub Actions의 Job을 실행하는 Runner는 크게 GitHub이 관리하는 GitHub-hosted Runner와 GitHub 외부에서 운영하는 self-hosted Runner 두 가지로 나뉘어요. 당근은 Kubernetes 환경에서 직접 운영하는 self-hosted Runner를 주로 사용하고 이 Runner는 ARC(Actions Runner Controller) 라는 Kubernetes 오퍼레이터로 관리해요. ARC는 Runner Scale Set 단위로 Runner를 관리하고 대기 중인 Job 수에 맞춰 Runner 수를 조절해요. Runner Scale Set에는 Runner의 이미지와 리소스 및 최소, 최대 수를 설정할 수 있고 Workflow의 runs-on에 Runner Scale Set을 지정하면 해당 Runner에 Job이 배정돼요. 출처: https://docs.github.com/en/actions/concepts/runners/actions-runner-controller Runner 수가 자동으로 조절되지만 모든 Job이 즉시 실행되지는 않고 GitHub 장애가 발생하거나 Job 요청이 급증해 실행이 지연되면 Queued 상태로 표시돼요. ARC로 Runner를 운영하면서 가장 자주 받은 문의도 “GitHub Action이 Queued 상태로 실행되지 않아요.”였어요. 하지만 상황 파악을 위한 데이터가 부족해서 GitHub 상태 페이지에 공지가 올라오기를 기다리거나 ARC가 기본적으로 제공하는 메트릭으로 원인을 추측할 수밖에 없었어요. ARC 기본 메트릭으로 Runner와 Job의 집계 현황은 볼 수 있지만 Runner를 기다리는 Job 개수와 대기 시간, 어떤 Job이 어느 Runner Pod에서 실행되는지는 파악하기 어려웠어요. 이런 정보를 확인할 수 있다면 Job 실행을 기다리는 개발자분들께 현재 상황을 더 명확하게 안내할 수 있을 거라고 생각했고 해결책을 찾던 중 Runner Pod에 Job 정보를 라벨로 추가하자는 ARC 이슈 를 발견했어요. 하지만 이 방식은 컨트롤러 변경과 권한 추가가 필요해 적용까지 시간이 걸릴 수 있었고 라벨을 메트릭으로 수집하는 구성도 따로 마련해야 해서 다른 방법을 찾아야 했어요. ⁠그래서 Runner Pod와 Job의 관계뿐만 아니라 대기 중인 Job까지 살펴볼 수 있도록 action-runner-job-exporter를 만들었어요. exporter는 Runner Pod에 Job 이름을 붙이는 Collector, Runner를 기다리는 Job을 추적하는 Webhook, Webhook의 상태를 저장하는 StateStore까지 세 개의 바이너리로 구성했어요. 지금부터 각 구성 요소를 만든 과정과 운영하며 개선한 내용을 소개할게요. action-runner-job-exporter 구조도 배경: ARC Runner가 생성되고 Job을 배정받기까지 Collector가 Runner와 Job을 어떻게 연결하는지 살펴보기 전에 ARC에서 Runner Pod가 생성되고 Job을 배정받는 과정을 먼저 알아볼게요. 각 Runner Scale Set의 Listener Pod는 GitHub과 세션을 맺고 새로운 Job 배정을 기다려요. 저장소에서 Workflow가 실행되면 GitHub은 각 Job의 runs-on에 맞는 Runner Scale Set에 Job을 배정해요. Listener는 배정된 Job과 최소·최대 Runner 설정을 바탕으로 필요한 Runner 수를 계산해서 EphemeralRunnerSet의 replicas를 변경해요. ARC가 필요한 수만큼 EphemeralRunner를 생성하고 GitHub에서 일회용 등록 설정(JIT config)을 받아와 Runner Pod를 띄워요. Runner Pod가 GitHub에 등록되면 GitHub은 해당 Runner에 Job을 배정해요. Job이 시작되면 Listener가 Job 배정 정보를 받아 해당 EphemeralRunner의 status 필드에 저장소와 Job 정보를 업데이트해요. Job이 끝나면 Runner 프로세스가 종료되고 ARC가 Runner 관련 리소스를 정리해요. Runner 생성, Job 배정 과정 ARC가 필요한 수만큼 Runner를 생성하면 각 Runner에 어떤 Job을 배정할지는 GitHub이 결정해요. Runner Pod는 특정 Job을 위해 생성되지 않으므로 Pod 이름만으로는 어떤 Job이 배정되었는지 알 수 없고 Listener가 EphemeralRunner의 status를 갱신해야 배정된 Job을 확인할 수 있어요. Collector: Runner Pod에 Job 이름 붙이기 exporter를 만든 목표는 개발자분들이 GitHub Actions의 상태를 문의하시기 전에 SRE가 GitHub Actions의 이상 징후를 먼저 파악하는 것이었어요. 그래서 가장 먼저 Runner Pod에서 어떤 Job을 실행하고 있는지 확인하고 싶었어요. Pod 라벨과 기존 메트릭에는 Job 정보가 없었지만 EphemeralRunner와 Runner Pod의 이름이 같다는 점을 이용하면 status에 기록된 Job 정보를 해당 Pod와 연결할 수 있다고 생각했어요. 이 아이디어로 Pod와 Job의 관계를 메트릭으로 확인할 수 있도록 첫 번째 바이너리인 Collector를 만들었어요. Collector는 Kubernetes informer로 EphemeralRunner의 생성, 변경, 삭제를 지켜보며 최신 상태를 메모리 캐시에 저장하고 이 캐시를 읽어 아래 메트릭을 제공해요. arc_runner_job_info{namespace, pod, runner_name, repository, job_name, workflow_ref, workflow_run_id} Collector는 Job이 시작되어 status.jobRepositoryName이 채워진 Runner에 대해서만 이 메트릭을 제공해요. workflow_run_id 라벨은 여러 Job을 이어서 작업을 정의하는 Workflow를 가리키는 값이라 https://github.com/<org>/<repo>/actions/runs/<workflow_run_id>로 실행 페이지 링크를 바로 만들 수 있게 구성했어요. Collector 구조도 Prometheus가 메트릭을 수집할 때 exporter Pod의 라벨과 이름이 겹쳐서 Runner Pod의 이름은 exported_pod에, Namespace는 exported_namespace에 담겨 있어요. 이 라벨을 컨테이너의 CPU, 메모리, 네트워크 사용량 메트릭(container_.*)에 있는 pod, namespace 라벨과 연결하면 사용량에 저장소와 Job 이름을 붙일 수 있어

title: Balancing Exploration and Exploitation in Constrained Combinatorial Optimization with U(1)-Symmetric Tensor Trains
abstract: Tensor Train (TT) decomposition has emerged as a powerful tool for mitigating the curse of dimensionality in a variety of machine learning and combinatorial optimization tasks. Recent advances show that TT-based generative models can efficiently represent and explore high-dimensional discrete spaces, even when the cost function structure is unknown. However, incorporating hard linear constraints into TT-based optimization remains challenging, as existing interpolation and sampling approaches often fail when feasible points are rare. In this work, we develop a general TT-based framework for constrained combinatorial optimization built upon U(1)-symmetric tensor networks. Our method introduces an expressibility-enhancement mechanism for constructing sparse symmetric tensors and a graph-based diversity measure that guides sample selection during training. On assignment benchmarks, expressibility enhancement and diversity-aware selection improve mean solution quality over their respective baselines. The assignment-selected diversifying strategy also extends to nonpolynomial Set Partitioning, with larger relative gains observed in the higher-tensor-rank data families. Separate runtime benchmarks show substantial speedups over ConstrainTNet and PROTES on non-degenerate assignment workloads; comparisons with simulated annealing depend on constraint information and computational budget, but, overall, support the practicality of the current implementation.

title: Do Diffusion Models Learn to Generalize Basic Visual Skills?
abstract: Diffusion models generate high-quality images, but how well they generalize is hard to measure. Current evaluations rely on human preference and prompt-following benchmarks for text-to-image models and on distribution-level metrics such as Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) and Inception Score (IS) for class-conditional models, but these cannot tell whether models learn basic visual skills or largely match training patterns. To address this gap, we introduce the Visual Generative Lab (VGL), a controlled experimental framework for studying how diffusion models learn and generalize basic visual skills, including size, position, rotation, count, color, shape, and their compositions. By generating synthetic training data for each skill from explicit rules, VGL allows precise measurement of generalization with task-specific, rule-based metrics. Training models from scratch on these data reveals three patterns in this controlled setting: (1) with our default design, extrapolation is limited: size and position degrade within a few pixels of the training range, count reaches only about 50% accuracy on out-of-range counts, and rotation extrapolation accuracy varies widely across seeds; (2) for compositional generalization, the number of distinct basic visual skill combinations matters more than dataset size; (3) skills mostly fail independently, except position. Code and data-generation scripts: https://github.com/AmishSethi/visual-generative-lab.

title: Fair Bubble Sort: Provably Optimal Fair Ranking with Continuous Sensitive Attributes
abstract: Most fair-ranking methods assume categorical protected attributes, requiring continuous attributes such as age or income to be discretized into groups. This introduces arbitrary thresholds, loses fine-grained information, and ignores the natural ordering of the attribute. In this paper, we study the problem of fair ranking with continuous protected attributes without relying on thresholding. We introduce Continuous Pairwise Parity (CPP), a fairness notion based on Kendall correlation between ranking positions and the protected attribute, and seek rankings that satisfy a prescribed CPP constraint while minimizing their Kemeny distance from an initial score-based ranking. To solve this problem, we propose Fair Bubble Sort (FBS), an efficient post-processing algorithm based on targeted adjacent swaps. We prove that FBS is exactly optimal for the unweighted Kemeny distance and provide approximation guarantees for the score-weighted setting. FBS is output-sensitive, with running time determined by the number of swaps required to meet the fairness constraint. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show that FBS is scalable and consistently outperforms discretization-based baselines, achieving a superior fairness-accuracy Pareto front.

title: BQ-LoRA: Binary-Quantized Low-Rank Adapters as Implicit Regularizers for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning
abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning of quantized large language models is dominated by QLoRA, which combines 4-bit weight quantization with FP16 low-rank adapters. We ask whether the FP16 adapter precision is necessary. Replacing it with a single binary bit per adapter parameter, combined with a learned per-layer scale $s$ and a Scaled Straight-Through Estimator, reduces adapter storage by 13-16x. We introduce two variants -- NormScale, which binarizes under a norm-preserving scale with a clipped STE, and LearnThresh, which makes the binarization threshold learnable -- unified under a framework we call BQ-LoRA. Our main theoretical contribution is a tight characterization of the BQ-LoRA hypothesis class: it has bounded entrywise norm, a typical-set spectral norm bound that is $Θ(r)$ times sharper than the worst case, a full-rank, near-isotropic update, and consequently a Rademacher complexity that yields an explicit $\tilde{O}(s_{\max}α\sqrt{d_{out}/(rn)})$ generalization bound. FP16 LoRA has no comparable a priori norm or isotropy control. On Qwen2.5 (1.5B-72B), BQ-LoRA exceeds QLoRA's benchmark averages at every scale by 0.8-3.5 points; on LLaMA-2 (7B/70B) it remains competitive at the same storage reduction but does not uniformly lead the strongest FP16-adapter baselines (LoftQ at 7B, QLoRA at 70B). On Qwen2.5-7B the binary adapter preserves the 4-bit base WikiText-2 PPL within 0.06 (9.86 vs. 9.80) while QLoRA worsens it by 0.59. The reduction applies to inference-time adapter storage and serving; training memory matches QLoRA and step time rises by under 4%. We translate the storage saving into a deployment study, BQ-SGMV, by extending Punica's SGMV kernel with a binary inner-product primitive: the same A100-80GB holds 15.6x more adapters in HBM, and our research prototype eliminates cache misses under a skewed synthetic workload.

title: Fidelity Regret: Measuring Simulator Misspecification in Verifiable Design
abstract: RLVF assumes the verifier evaluates the quantity of interest. In genetic-circuit design, a topological verifier can establish that a program is a valid circuit computing the target function, whereas ranking its physical performance requires a simulator. We measure fidelity regret, the reference simple regret incurred when a cheap simulator selects the design, over a 21,362-design combination subspace spanning 5 measured gate libraries and 3 organisms. Exact ordered-assignment checks retain positive regret in every tested cell while shifting magnitudes in both directions. Mean normalized regret is 0.369 over 72 cells and only 6 have zero regret. The discrepancy depends strongly on the reference axis: the yeast library SC1C1G1T1 has mean regret 0.113 for cytometry quality and 0.801 for growth burden, and every evaluated library--circuit-size pair has positive burden regret. Topological verification ties all valid gate assignments, while an oracle whitelist subject to retaining at least 25% of the design space leaves positive regret in 30 of 52 cells. Design-space optimization and feedback-guided search with frozen language models reach the high-regret regions; on a matched zero-regret control, additional optimization instead reduces regret. At a matched modeled-cost budget, mitigation is budget- and library-dependent. An in-sample fixed rule spending $α{=}0.34$ of the budget re-scoring top cheap-simulator designs achieves mean excess regret 0.016, compared with 0.305 for cheap-only and 0.034 for reference-only selection, improving on cheap-only in 330 of 360 cells. More broadly, any workflow optimized through a simulator or digital twin can satisfy its verifier yet perform poorly on the intended physical objective. Fidelity regret provides a transferable template for detecting this gap before optimization and comparing budget-aware remedies across scientific domains.

title: RAG in a Trenchcoat: When Minimal Memory Is Enough for Agentic Systems, and When It Isn't
abstract: Agentic memory research has accumulated extraction, supersession, reflection, and graph synthesis on top of retrieval-augmented generation. However, we found that almost none of those primitives earn their cost in our tested memory benchmarks: we show this with BRIDGE, a deliberately minimal RAG memory with chained observation notes, hybrid BM25 with cosine retrieval, and chronological rendering, which reaches parity within bootstrap CI with the prior SOTA on LongMemEval-S and BEAM, and beats the best memory baseline on EverMemBench by 5.7-6.3 points at matched reader. It runs at ~5-7K reader-prompt tokens per query, using a single LLM call for each ingestion or query. We argue that this parity is itself the result: standard benchmarks score what memory retrieves, not what memory enables when the agent acts. To test the latter, we introduce five adversarial probes (Rule Application +-, Pattern Induction Style / Procedural, Dynamic Multiturn) judged at generation time by a cross vendor verification chain, where each query can only be solved by applying a remembered rule or pattern it never mentions. Across 5 probes x 20 scenarios, no architecture wins universally: atomic fact extractors (LangMem) win rule application, while BRIDGE's block-summary memory wins pattern induction. This result holds across four domains, three graders, and three reader families. Each design fails where the other wins, for reasons a recall benchmark cannot see: atomic-fact extractors discard the form a demonstrated pattern takes, while block-summary memory retrieves the rule but the reader does not act on it, a gap that presenting the rule more prominently largely closes. What separates memory designs is not what they retrieve but what they enable an agent to do, and that is what agentic memory should be evaluated on.

title: Reconfiguring Procedural Knowledge for Compositional Robot Skill Adaptation
abstract: General-purpose behavior models increasingly internalize broad procedural knowledge during training, making their adaptation to new goals and skill interfaces less a problem of learning entirely new behaviors than of reconfiguring existing competence. We study this capability as reconfigurability, the ability to realize new behaviors by cost-efficiently restructuring existing components and relations under sparse governing information, where task specifications provide high-level goals and procedure specifications expose a limited set of reusable factors, leaving the concrete bindings and compositions required for execution underdetermined. We propose RecPo, a framework that represents skills task-agnostically through multiple procedure views and materializes executable skill sequences by composing stored transitions to realize task-specific changes. RecPo maintains a procedure knowledge base of skill-induced transitions, with each view exposing a reusable factor and preserving local skill connectivity. At deployment, it interprets task specifications through the same views and resolves the resulting compositional queries over the stored relations to bind skills for execution. On long-horizon tasks in an extended Franka Kitchen benchmark, RecPo achieves 91.9% ordered completion with 1.0 ms of task inference per episode across varying procedure support and task-record sparsity. Real-robot studies further demonstrate adaptation through local memory edits without task-specific retraining.

title: Towards Optimism-Pessimism Trade-off in Model-based Offline-to-Online Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Model-based offline-to-online reinforcement learning (RL) enables sample-efficient adaptation by leveraging offline pre-training for online fine-tuning. However, the distribution shifts between offline and online stages often hinder fine-tuning performance. Many existing methods encode the optimism-pessimism trade-off through a single-objective formulation. Selecting its trade-off coefficient through online fine-tuning can require costly bi-level optimization. We identify the balance established during offline training as a key challenge: in our motivating experiments, optimistic policies adapt better to novel tasks, whereas pessimistic policies perform better on the same online tasks. To address this challenge, we propose a bi-objective formulation that captures this trade-off, yielding a Pareto policy pool during offline training. This policy pool enables adaptive selection during online fine-tuning across diverse online tasks. To generate the pool, we introduce Multi-Objective Soft Actor-critIC (MOSAIC), which solves bi-objective problems and constructs diverse Pareto policies. After offline training, a contextual bandit algorithm hierarchically selects the most suitable policy for fine-tuning at each online interaction step. Empirically, our pipeline, Hierarchical Pareto Policy Pool (HiP3), achieves the strongest aggregate performance across both same and novel online tasks and maintains its advantage under stronger distribution shifts. Comprehensive ablations further clarify the roles of the policy pool, MOSAIC-based pool construction, and the online selection mechanism.

title: Long-Context Generation Is a Sampling Problem (When You Turn Up the Heat)
abstract: Open-weight language models are widely observed to get worse the longer they generate. Often, attempts to fix this involve more training. At high temperature, The sampler, i.e. the rule that picks the next token out of the model's probabilities, decides whether long and agentic generation survives and/or thrives. We test 29 open-weight models from 1B to 122B parameters on ten established benchmarks plus needle retrieval out to one million tokens, covering SWE-bench Verified coding agents, long chain-of-thought reasoning, long-form writing, long structured output and long-context reading. Samplers that keep their pool of candidate tokens small and steady as temperature rises don't lose accuracy. Samplers that let in low-probability tokens fall apart. At temperature 2, coding agents running top-p, top-k or Top-H resolve 0 of 100 GitHub issues, while the same agents running top-nsigma resolve 46 to 62 and win every issue the two samplers disagree on, on three Qwen3.5 models. Over all benchmarks top-nsigma keeps a median 100% of its temperature-1 score where top-p keeps 26%. Counting how many tokens each sampler lets through explains why. In one Llama-3.1-8B story, going from temperature 1 to 2 grows top-p's pool from 4 tokens to 51,845 while top-nsigma stays at 3. Across 133 combinations of sampler setting and temperature, the typical pool size predicts judged quality (Spearman correlation of -0.77), and when we pick the pool at temperature 1 and only apply temperature afterwards, Top-H, min-p and p-less stop collapsing. At the default temperature of 1 most samplers perform about the same, We release all code and data to the public.

title: Synthetic Crystal Data Generation for Diffusion Pretraining in Material Property Prediction
abstract: Diffusion-based pretraining has emerged as a powerful strategy for learning transferable representations in graph neural networks for materials property prediction without requiring quantum-mechanical labels such as energies, forces, and stresses for every pretraining structure. However, the method retains a critical dependency: it requires structures residing near local minima of a potential energy surface, which have traditionally been obtained through costly DFT relaxations of known or physically synthesized compounds. This reliance constrains both the scale and the structural diversity of available pretraining data, leaving large regions of crystal structure space unexplored. In this work, we connect diffusion-based pretraining with synthetic structure generation to reduce this bottleneck. We introduce a synthetic data generation pipeline combining three complementary strategies: perturb-and-relax, generative sampling via MatterGen, and protostructure enumeration. Where structural relaxation is required, we use fast machine-learned interatomic potentials instead of performing a new DFT relaxation for each generated structure. We further compare a coordinate-denoising control with continuous-time variance-preserving (VP) and sub-VP diffusion objectives using a randomly initialized Orb-v2 backbone. The source comparison covers seven MatBench property-prediction tasks, and an eighth task, \texttt{mp\_gap}, is included in the protostructure scaling study. Every synthetic-pretraining condition numerically outperforms random initialization on all seven source-comparison tasks. Scaling the protostructure corpus from 20k to 165k under a fixed 400-epoch schedule numerically matches or exceeds MP-20k pretraining on most tasks; because this protocol increases both data diversity and optimization updates, the result reflects joint data-and-compute scaling.

title: ReMoE: An Interpretable Mixture-of-Experts Framework for Human Mobility Recovery Forecasting Across Disasters
abstract: Human mobility often declines sharply following disasters and subsequently exhibits complex recovery dynamics. Effective forecasting of this recovery is critical for timely assessment and resource allocation. However, existing approaches are often developed for individual events and operate as black boxes, limiting their transferability and interpretability beyond the events they were trained on. Recent studies have identified recurring post-disaster mobility recovery types across disasters, suggesting that recovery knowledge may be transferable. Motivated by this, we propose ReMoE, an interpretable mixture-of-experts framework for cross-disaster mobility recovery forecasting. ReMoE uses a feature-guided router to adaptively combine specialized experts that learn these heterogeneous yet reusable recovery types, producing a region-specific recovery pattern. It further refines this pattern through residual correction informed by forecasts of future hazard conditions. We evaluate ReMoE on a large-scale mobility dataset covering 18 disaster events spanning hurricanes, floods, winter storms, and wildfires. ReMoE is competitive in-distribution and achieves the strongest performance on unseen events and hazard types, with larger gains under greater distribution shifts. Further analyses show that ReMoE yields interpretable learning outcomes and maintains robust performance under uncertainty. Broadly, ReMoE offers a transferable and traceable forecaster that can support anticipatory post-disaster assessment.

title: Every Measurement, Every Direction, All at Once: Multimodal Flow Matching for Molecules and Spectra
abstract: Generative modeling in science is often data-limited, where experiments are expensive. However, each experiment may yield several coupled measurements of the same physical entity. Standard generative models often train only on a single direction, discarding supervision from the rest. We argue that each experiment contains more training signal than this asymmetry allows the model to exploit: random masking enables measurements to serve as either conditioning inputs or prediction targets, yielding multiple supervised denoising tasks from a single experiment. We investigate this premise with MOSAIC, a multimodal flow matching transformer over molecular 3D structure and UV, IR, and Raman spectra. MOSAIC is a single model that is capable of any-to-any generation: generating any subset of modalities from any disjoint subset of the others. On QM9S, MOSAIC achieves 88.8% molecular graph recovery, outperforming the strongest spectra-to-structure baseline by 23.2% in structure generation, while simultaneously outperforming a structure-to-spectra specialist model in spectral generation. Ablations show that the any-to-any objective improves structure generation over structure-only training across model sizes. Furthermore, MOSAIC supports arbitrary subsets of available measurements and enables molecular identification by matching generated spectra to experimental references.

title: Addressing Exogenous Variability in Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) often fails under exogenous variability such as shifts in opponents or environment regimes that cannot be controlled by the team but alter the transition dynamics. We formalize this challenge as Exogenous Dec-POMDP (ED-POMDP), in which an episode-level exogenous regime, selected independently of the team, indexes the dynamics, and the global state is partitioned into components that are directly responsive to the current team action and components that are not directly action-responsive at the current step. This formulation exposes mediated influence: while team actions do not directly update the latter at the current step, they can shape their later evolution through induced changes in the former. Based on this, we propose LEICA, a CTDE-compatible algorithm that learns history-conditioned context representations for both components and shapes policy updates using agent-wise, influence-weighted counterfactual intrinsic rewards. Across SMAX benchmarks with opponent strategy shifts, LEICA consistently improves both training performance and generalization to unseen opponents' strategies over existing baselines, supporting the usefulness of influence-weighted shaping under exogenous train-test regime shifts.

title: Solver to System: LLM Reasoning Across Representations and Execution in Scientific Simulation
abstract: Simulators based on partial differential equations (PDEs) are widely used to model physical systems, but generating and interpreting PDE solver code with large language models (LLMs) remains challenging. Scientific simulation code is a useful testbed for LLM scientific reasoning because (1) one system can be represented by code, equations, natural language, and numerical trajectories and (2) code can execute successfully while implementing invalid physics. We introduce Solver2System, a dataset of PDE solvers with multiple representations, controlled corruptions, and lexical perturbations, to evaluate whether LLMs can recover the underlying physical system through (1) cross-representation consistency and (2) static and agentic detection of physical invalidity. Across eight open-weight models, LLMs systematically favor some representations when evidence conflicts, and lexical perturbations to code alter interpretation of other unchanged representations. Execution improves physical-validity judgments, but weaker agents can judge correctly without identifying the causal defect. Thus, LLMs may reach correct judgments despite inconsistent representation reconciliation or causal misdiagnosis.

title: World-Grounded Reinforcement Learning for Pollution-Aware Bird Movement Modeling Using a Multi-Instance DQN Framework
abstract: Birds are modeled as environmentally sensitive agents whose movement reflects real-world air quality conditions, where AQI serves as a measurable world feedback signal representing pollution-driven consequences. Instead of relying on human preference or synthetic rewards, the system uses environmental outcomes as the primary training signal, enabling policy learning grounded in ecological impact. We propose a multi-instance reinforcement learning simulation in which agents navigate a 2D grid representation of India integrated with a precomputed AQI matrix and geographic state boundaries. The framework combines bird call metadata from the Xeno-canto dataset, spatial discretization, and real environmental data to learn adaptive navigation strategies under pollution constraints. To ensure scalability and efficiency, repeated real-time API queries are replaced by a structured AQI mapping that enables fast lookup during training and execution. Multiple baselines, including Monte Carlo, Q-Learning, and Value Iteration, are evaluated for comparison. Deep Q-Network demonstrates stronger stability, adaptability, and cumulative performance across varying environmental conditions, establishing a scalable foundation for world-feedback driven ecological decision modeling.

title: The Hidden Cost of MoE Diffusion Decoding: Profiling and Fixing the Sampler
abstract: Masked diffusion language models (dLLMs) decode by iteratively denoising a full canvas of tokens, so every forward pass runs a per-token sampling and stopping pipeline over the entire canvas-by-vocabulary logits tensor. We profile single-user decoding of a 26B-parameter diffusion Mixture-of-Experts model on a bandwidth-bound edge accelerator (NVIDIA GB10) and report a result that is easy to miss: after weight quantisation, this logits pipeline, not the expert GEMMs, is the single largest consumer of decode time. Unlike autoregressive decoding, where sampling touches one position's logits per committed token, diffusion decoding processes S times as many logit entries per output token, where S is the number of denoising steps. We show this pipeline is largely redundant or fusable and remove it in two lossless tiers: a bit-exact tier whose output is byte-identical to the reference decoder, and an accuracy-parity tier using a fused single-pass entropy kernel and Gumbel-max sampling. Combined with a W4A16 expert kernel, the full stack reaches 2.4-2.7 times end-to-end speedup over bf16 at unchanged benchmark accuracy on GSM8K, HumanEval, and MATH, on a single 273 GB/s device. We confirm the finding on a second, independently built diffusion MoE (LLaDA2.0-mini: pipeline 28.8% of decode, fused W4A16 3.3 times at accuracy parity) and show it disappears on a dense diffusion model (3.6%). The cost is specific to MoE diffusion, where quantisation makes the backbone cheap. Code and quantised weights are released.

title: When Does Discrete Ricci Curvature Help? An Edge-Level Analysis of Curvature-Enhanced GCNs for PPI Prediction
abstract: Curvature-enhanced graph convolutional networks (CGCN) incorporate Ollivier-Ricci curvature (ORC), grounded in optimal transport theory, into message passing, motivated by the claim that curvature-weighted edges alleviate "over-squashing" at structural bottlenecks. But does CGCN's improvement actually come from mitigating over-squashing? We investigate this on four real-world protein-protein interaction (PPI) datasets, comparing CGCN against a standard GCN at the level of individual edges rather than aggregate metrics alone. While CGCN improves aggregate AUC, AUPR, and F1 across all four datasets, this gain is concentrated almost entirely on low-degree edges, while performance on low-curvature (bottleneck) edges systematically degrades in three of four datasets, the opposite of what the over-squashing motivation predicts. Examining the learned edge-weight function directly, together with clustering-validity metrics, edge-distance ratios, and a layer-depth ablation across four depths, we find evidence for an alternative account: curvature-weighting sharpens the separation between clusters, which improves intra-cluster predictions at the cost of inter-cluster (bottleneck) ones. We test this account against topologically defined communities rather than the classification labels used elsewhere. Additionally, we offer practical guidance on when to prefer CGCN over standard GCN, depending on whether intra- or inter-cluster predictions matter most.

title: Learning Calibrated and Samplable Predictive Distributions of Surface-Ocean $Δp$CO$_2$ Using Tabular Diffusion Models
abstract: The ocean absorbs almost 30% of anthropogenic CO$_2$ emissions, but quantifying this sink requires estimating surface-ocean CO$_2$ from observations that are sparse in space and time. Most existing machine-learning estimates of this field are deterministic, giving a single value per grid point, with uncertainty approximated post hoc via residuals, ensembles, or prescribed distributions. We instead learn a conditional predictive distribution for each observation: using Treeffuser, a conditional diffusion model with gradient-boosted-tree score functions, we estimate the full predictive distribution of $Δp$CO$_2$ (the sea-air $p$CO$_2$ difference) from 13 environmental, spatial, and temporal predictors. On a held-out SOCAT test set, Treeffuser attains the lowest continuous ranked probability score among the uncertainty-quantification methods evaluated (8.229 $μ$atm) and the coverage closest to the nominal 68% / 95% levels (0.686 / 0.930), while retaining point-prediction skill comparable to a deterministic XGBoost baseline (RMSE 18.4 vs. 17.7 $μ$atm; $R^2$ 0.77 vs. 0.79). These results show that conditional diffusion can provide well-calibrated, observation-level uncertainties while largely preserving point-prediction skill. Because Treeffuser is generative, its samples can support probabilistic analyses of $Δp$CO$_2$; extending this to spatially coherent field reconstruction will require modeling dependence across grid cells and evaluation on spatially held-out data.

title: Optimistic Verifiers Get Hacked: Reward Hacking Under an Exact Process Oracle
abstract: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards inherits whatever its verifier gets wrong. Outside mathematics and code the verifier is a proxy, a rubric, a learned judge or a hand-written checker, and its distance from the true objective is never measured, so a rising reward cannot be told apart from a hack. We build a setting where the true reward is exactly computable at the process level: executable authorization policies over 124,416 contexts admit an oracle that lists every minimal sufficient reason for every decision. We compile these policies into exact process rewards, degrade the verifier along seven realistic axes (outcome-only, sufficiency, recall-only, extraction noise, coarse taxonomy, stale policy, LLM judge), and train against each while the exact verifier scores every rollout. Four phenotypes appear. Optimistic verifiers are hacked by padding: the sufficiency proxy ends at 0.940 while true faithfulness falls from 0.731 to 0.667 on 96 held-out episodes. Outcome-only verifiers saturate and stop teaching, noise dilutes, and ranking-preserving gaps do no harm. A model-free audit of the verifier, its selection error and gap sign, together with a short saturation pilot, anticipates which phenotype a run will produce. Across nine configurations spanning two frameworks, two model vendors, two adapter sizes, three precisions, two initialisations and two seeds, the phenotypes recur, sufficiency damage is positive in all 10 replication cells and beyond two standard errors in 7, and optimistic gaps remain the steeper branch. The damage magnitude does not replicate, and five pre-registered attempts to explain it are reported as they fell. We release the testbed, the training instrumentation, and 14 real public policies (Cedar, OPA, Gatekeeper) ported to executable oracles.

title: Differentiable Exact Learning
abstract: We introduce a framework for differentiable exact learning that couples an unbounded external environment to a state-tracking neural controller, which we train on policy-trajectory observations (PTOs): expert behavior traces that expose observations and actions while hiding internal states. In addition to the learning framework, we introduce Differentiable Finite-State Transducers (DFSTs) which use multilinear updates, support log-parallel training, and emulate arbitrary finite-state controllers, yielding computational universality through environmental interaction. From tiny training datasets, compact DFSTs achieve extreme length generalization on arithmetic and universal-simulation tasks. We replicate the success of DFSTs on RNNs and GRUs, thereby supporting a broader learning recipe: State-Tracking Controller + Unbounded External Environment + PTOs = Extreme Length Generalization. Beyond length generalization, our metric-extraction protocol recovers interpretable discrete controllers from trained DFSTs, which we prove equivalent to the target arithmetic and universal-simulation algorithms. Furthermore, for our Softmax DFST models, simply taking $\mathrm{argmax}$ over the transition probabilities yields discrete controllers which provably exactly perform universal Turing-machine simulation and binary arithmetic. Proving exact learning for the neural controllers requires assumptions, which we empirically support. We make our code, training recipes, model weights, and proof checkers publicly available at https://github.com/fanagor/DEL.

title: Subprocess-Constrained Markov Decision Processes
abstract: Constrained Markov decision processes (CMDPs) typically bound expected cumulative cost from an initial state. Such a guarantee can be insufficient when a policy must remain feasible after every history it may encounter. We introduce \emph{subprocess-constrained MDPs} (S-CMDPs), which require the expected discounted cost of each continuation, conditional on any reachable history, to satisfy a bound determined by the current state. This stronger requirement changes the structure and complexity of the problem: we show that stationary policies can be strictly suboptimal, and finding even an approximately optimal stationary policy is NP-hard. We adapt a recently introduced value-set iteration framework to show that history-dependent policies surprisingly overcome both obstacles. Our polynomial-time algorithm represents such a policy implicitly: its expected reward is within $ε$ of the optimal feasible value, it violates each subprocess cost bound by at most $δ$, and its action distribution can be computed in polynomial time for any given history.

title: Variational Monte Carlo for Quantum Excited States via Nested Low-Rank Approximation
abstract: The electronic Schrödinger equation encodes a molecule's electronic structure and quantum properties, but solving it scales exponentially with the number of electrons. Solving this equation with neural-network variational Monte Carlo (VMC) has reached chemical accuracy on the ground state of small molecules; extending this success to excited states is constrained by two existing paradigms. Penalty-based methods need $K$ Laplacians per step but require tuning the overlap-penalty weights against the energy gaps they aim to compute. Natural excited states VMC (NES-VMC) is penalty-free, but it combines the $K$ ansatzes into one determinant, whose local energy requires $K^2$ Laplacians per step. We resolve this trade-off via low-rank approximation (LoRA) reparameterization of the rank-$K$ variational objective. The reparameterized objective admits a VMC-compatible stochastic gradient estimator via MCMC sampling from the per-state Born densities, and a sequential nesting scheme recovers the lowest $K$ eigenstates in eigenvalue order. The resulting algorithm, NestedLoRA-VMC, inherits a global optimality guarantee from the LoRA principle. On the first-row atoms Li through Ne at $K=10$, its accuracy is comparable to that of NES-VMC and of a state-of-the-art penalty-based method.

title: Shaping AI's Beliefs Before It Generates: Human Sense of Agency in Creative AI
abstract: AI systems for creative media generation expand human capabilities yet risk diminishing human agency. A core problem is anchoring, where the user's thinking becomes anchored to a polished, generated artifact, shifting the user's role from active authoring to reactive editing. We propose pre-generation belief controls that can empower creators to inspect, revise, and steer the AI's interpretation before any media is generated, so that the initial anchor is set by the human. We formalize four design principles and instantiate them in the Proactive Co-Creator (PaCC), a system for early-stage conceptual ideation and prototyping that proactively surfaces its assumptions and uncertainty through clarifications, belief graphs, and media attributes, inviting users to shape the AI's beliefs before generating the final outcome. Using PaCC as a design probe in a small-scale, single-arm exploratory user study, we observed that participants reported directionally positive sense of agency and process control relative to their familiar prompt-based AI tools, noting that surfaced assumptions helped them think through details they had overlooked, whereas their feelings about ownership and authorship diverged

title: The Mask Is Not the Object: Volumetric Supervision for 3D Gaussian Segmentation
abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting enables object-level operations on Gaussian primitives, yet existing segmentation methods are largely trained and evaluated through rendered views. This mismatch can produce accurate rendered masks from incomplete 3D selections since alpha-blended feature supervision concentrates learning on dominant contributors while leaving occluded or low-contribution Gaussians weakly supervised. We propose VODA, a plug-and-play supervision objective that exploits local depth structure to group per-pixel contributors and directly supervises all Gaussians in selected depth clusters, bypassing contribution-weighted gradient delivery. To evaluate volumetric completeness, we introduce Removal-3D, a synthetic object-removal benchmark, and the Removal Depth Error (RDE), a metric comparing predicted and ground-truth depth changes. Across four rendering-based baselines, VODA consistently improves volumetric segmentation on Removal-3D while maintaining or improving performance on LERF and ScanNet. Further analysis shows that VODA recovers lower-contribution Gaussians, while simple gradient reweighting and spatial propagation fail to reproduce comparable gains.

title: The Price of Choosing Examples: Context Overfitting in Adaptive In-Context Learning
abstract: In-context learning is usually analyzed as if the examples in the prompt were sampled before the learner is chosen. In deployed systems they are not: examples are retrieved, filtered, re-ranked, edited, and repeatedly tested after seeing the query and the data store. We formalize this gap by treating prompt construction as adaptive data analysis through a conditional stochastic-kernel calculus. Our main quantity is the context capacity, the mutual information or approximate max-information between the data store and the final prompt transcript. For any frozen in-context learner and any adaptive context pipeline with capacity $κ$, we prove a finite-sample context generalization bound of order $\sqrt{κ/k}$, where $k$ is the number of selected examples whose losses form the reported score. We prove a matching lower bound, whose constant is exact when $\log k\llκ\ll k$, and derive two PAC-Bayesian retrieval rules: a first-order Gibbs rule that charges data-dependent candidate gates their prior mass, and a self-normalized second-order rule. On Banking77 with 64 retrieval recipes and two model families, the certificates hold in all 24,000 resampled selection events, and from 64 (Qwen2.5-7B) or 128 (GPT-4.1-mini) reused validation queries the Gibbs rule certifies a risk below the zero-shot error in over 99% of validation draws. Finally, we instantiate the theory for Bayesian linear in-context regression, including an order-statistics analysis of query-aligned top-$k$ Gaussian retrieval. The results separate context quality from context certification: longer or more relevant contexts improve risk only when the procedure used to choose them is stable enough for selected-context evidence to transfer.

title: Anytime-Valid PAC-Bayes Certificates for Adaptive Test-Time Scaling
abstract: Test-time scaling systems often choose how much to sample, which prompt to use, and which verifier or aggregation rule to trust after repeatedly inspecting a calibration set. Standard validation error bars are not valid after this adaptive selection. We model a test-time scaling recipe as a randomized predictor with a random cost and prove a time-uniform PAC-Bayes certificate that holds simultaneously over all calibration times, all posterior mixtures over recipes, and all data-dependent stopping rules. Thus the same event covers the recipe search that precedes deployment, not merely the fixed recipe finally reported. For a finite grid of budgets and verifiers, the penalty is the familiar $\log M/n$, which in the worst case no certificate valid after selection can avoid, while non-uniform priors and localized posterior mixtures can give sharper certificates for structured searches. We specialize the result to self-consistency and show a complementary margin law: plurality voting improves exponentially in the sample budget only on examples where the correct answer is the generator's unique mode; otherwise more compute can provably amplify errors. The same margin analysis yields an oracle water-filling law for compute allocation. A synthetic audit quantifies the optimism caused by adaptive budget selection, and a 192-example GSM8K audit using gpt-4.1-mini generations illustrates risk-cost reporting for a real inference pipeline. At scale, with two models on GSM8K and MATH-500, selected-best error bars fall below the out-of-split GSM8K risk in up to 22.5% of random splits at a nominal 5% while the certificate never does, and on the full GSM8K test split it tightens to 0.109 (held-out risk 0.039). The results give a lightweight, distribution-free way to report risk and compute claims for adaptive inference systems.

title: Out-of-training properties in frozen interatomic potential embeddings are decodable and ordered by physical scale
abstract: Machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) are trained on energies, forces and stresses, yet their frozen representations can predict other materials properties. We probe ORB-v3 and UMA-S across layers, read-outs and equivariant channels for nine properties of 154,875 Materials Project crystals. Both models outperform composition-only descriptors on all targets, including five outside their training objectives; errors in physical units help assess potential screening applications. Optimal depth varies by property, consistent with a physical-scale ordering. Random-weight controls reveal strongly property-dependent benefits of pretraining. UMA-S's rotation-invariant angular channels improve crystal-system classification, while higher scores from its full tensor disappear under rotation; matched-model controls do not isolate equivariance as the explanation. Accuracy varies across different probes, but nearest-neighbour prediction often approaches XGBoost performance, even though materials do not form distinct clusters according to their properties. We also test whether a linear predictor trained on one model's embeddings can predict properties using the other model's embeddings after a learned linear transformation. Predictive accuracy is largely preserved, despite differences in which atoms the two models place close together. These results guide the reuse of frozen MLIP representations for materials prediction.

title: SemiNovo: Learning Beyond Search-Identified Spectra for De Novo Peptide Sequencing
abstract: Sensitive peptide identification is fundamental to protein characterization and novel protein discovery, for which de novo peptide sequencing (DNPS) from tandem mass spectra provides an important database-independent approach. Although deep learning has substantially advanced de novo sequencing, existing models are predominantly trained on high-confidence peptide-spectrum matches obtained through database search. This search-conditioned supervision excludes a large fraction of unidentified spectra, creating a distribution mismatch between the selectively labeled training data and the complete spectrum stream encountered at inference time, thereby limiting peptide identification performance. To address this challenge, we propose SemiNovo, a semi-supervised framework that learns jointly from identified and unlabeled spectra. SemiNovo first constructs DarkSpec, a large-scale quality-controlled corpus of unlabeled spectra collected from diverse public proteomics projects, thereby extending training beyond search-identified spectra and mitigating the resulting shift in DNPS supervision. It then combines stepwise mass-constrained autoregressive decoding with cumulative path confidence to derive reliable supervision from unlabeled spectra. Moreover, SemiNovo introduces head-wise chemical-evidence gating to improve spectral evidence aggregation under noisy and incomplete fragmentation. Experiments show that SemiNovo performs favorably against state-of-the-art methods on multiple benchmarks. Code and dataset are publicly available.

title: Does the Voice Matter? Evaluating Frustration Detection on Deployed Clinical Voice-Agent Calls
abstract: Autonomous voice agents now conduct routine clinical follow-up calls, so some automated triage is unavoidable. A patient becoming frustrated is one thing that triage should catch. These systems typically read only the transcript the speech-to-text stage produces, not the voice, and whether that is enough is largely untested on real clinical speech. We study per-turn frustration detection on real patient calls from a deployed clinical voice agent: 150 turns from six calls labelled by three annotators, with a length-matched acted corpus as a control, and 714 turns from 30 calls. Patient turns are overwhelmingly short: across the deployed calls, roughly 59% are one or two words, against 13% in the full acted corpus, and a corpus accuracy gap remains even after the acted set is length-matched. On one-word turns, transcript-only detection does not exclude chance. Across five audio-capable language models, the transcript flags 3 or 4 of the 39 frustrated one-word turns in the 30 calls, and a classifier given only the word count reaches 57.3%. Whether audio helps depends on the model and on the instruction. Asked to attend to delivery, two Gemini 2.5 models gain 3.0 pp over the transcript across 30 calls (-1.0 to 7.5 pp). Of the turns they confidently clear, 6.9% were in fact frustrated for audio against 13.0% for the transcript, a difference of 6.1 pp (2.2 to 10.4 pp). Across the 30 calls, given one prompt identical for both inputs, no model's audio-text interval excludes zero. Under the input-specific prompts, a newer Gemini model and two smaller open models do worse with audio than with the transcript (-3.5, -8.6 and -10.6 pp). A WavLM probe trained on the clinical calls matches the best prompted model overall (71.6%) but misses every frustrated one-word turn in the 24 added calls. When a patient's turn is short, the transcript alone is not enough to rule out frustration.

title: CONGA: Compiling Gaussian Fiber Geometry for Structured Bayesian Inference
abstract: In structured Bayesian models, a large latent block is often Gaussian conditional on a smaller set of parameters, yet generic inference methods relearn this geometry during warmup. We study how this structure can be used to construct transports for posterior inference. The conditional mean and precision determine exact affine maps, including symmetric Brenier and triangular Knothe-Rosenblatt maps, that separate a standard normal block from the remaining non-Gaussian core. KL and relative Fisher objectives then reduce to objectives on this core. We introduce CONGA, a compiler that identifies candidate Gaussian blocks and selects a temporal, spectral, or sparse implementation according to their structure and computational cost. Marginalization requires an identity established from the model; numerical evidence alone permits only a target-preserving change of variables, and a failed check leaves the model unchanged. On the Stock-Watson inflation model, CONGA improves minimum ESS per second by 12.5x for NUTS. It also restores convergence where the raw target fails: for WALNUTS on the same model, and for NUTS on a 6760-dimensional electricity load model reduced to 34 core coordinates. Experiments on graph-indexed fields show how coloring and fill affect the choice of map, including cases where retaining the original target is preferable. Code at https://github.com/vicgalle/conga

title: Living Context Graphs: Continual Semantic Learning for Enterprise Data Reasoning
abstract: Enterprise AI can now perform analytics, reporting, and data-driven workflows, yet the data foundations it relies on remain hard to operationalize: business meaning, relationships, metric definitions, and reporting conventions are absent from database schemas and scattered across undocumented systems and tribal knowledge. We introduce the Living Context Graph (LCG), a continually learned context layer that makes existing enterprise data operational for AI without requiring a copy or transformation of the underlying warehouse. LCG bootstraps base semantics and relationships from the data itself, builds a concept graph that indexes business context as queries are served, writes durable semantic learnings from verified outcomes, and withdraws or re-earns context when later outcomes contradict prior routes. We evaluate LCG through text-to-SQL, a core data-reasoning task, on a transfer-aware split of three BIRD databases comprising 499 questions: 353 form the learning history and 146 are held out and never used to update the context layer. Bootstrapping alone improves overall accuracy by +4.6 percentage points. Learning only from the history raises accuracy on the untouched held-out transfer set by +22.6 points (95% CI [+14.4, +30.8]), exceeding five-shot retrieval from the same history by +12.3 points. Incremental learning reaches the one-shot endpoint within observed evaluation noise on every database. Ablating the graph changes held-out accuracy by at most one question per database but increases per-query cost 2.3-3.3x and median latency 1.8-3.4x: continually learned semantics drive accuracy, while the graph makes that context efficient to serve.

title: DetourBench: Trajectory-Level Evaluation of Interactive Agents with Exact Minimum-Action Bounds
abstract: Benchmarks judge language-model agents mainly by whether they reach the correct final state, not by how they got there. Endpoint scoring cannot separate an agent that retrieved exactly the evidence a decision required from one that read most of the environment, nor an agent that never located the evidence from one that stopped a single action short. Settling this needs a reference cost, and authored solutions establish only that a task is solvable, not that no shorter route exists. We present DetourBench, which constrains the environment until that minimum is computable. Each task is a finite, partially observable transition system with unit-cost accesses whose resources become globally addressable after discovery. Exhaustive search yields the full-information minimum action count $L_0$ with a replayable witness; from graph-recoverable terminal states it also yields exact residual work $R_T$, which separates an episode that stopped one access short from one that wandered, while an irreversible wrong commitment is recorded as having no finite residual distance rather than assigned one. Success, attainment, residual progress, and normalized detour are reported separately. Across 375 scored episodes --- five model endpoints, 25 integrated tasks, three repeats --- success ranges from 58.7% to 96.0% while conditional attainment ranges from 0.803 to 0.890 and orders the models differently. Among recoverable failures, residual work separates near-complete trajectories from costly incompletion and from irreversible commitment. We open-source the instances, oracle witnesses, and evaluation harness at https://github.com/DatagridsAI/DetourBench.

title: MSAR: Next-Scale Autoregressive Forecasting for Time Series via Modular Multi-Scale Decoupling
abstract: Time series forecasting underpins critical applications in finance, energy, healthcare, and transportation. Although deep models have achieved strong results, most adopt single-scale modeling or restrict multiscale processing to the input side, causing a misalignment between multiscale inputs and single-scale outputs and limiting predictive power. We introduce the Modular Scale-wise Autoregressive Framework (MSAR), a model-agnostic design that forecasts progressively across multiple temporal resolutions. MSAR offers three advantages: (1) scale-wise aligned modeling, which disentangles heterogeneous temporal patterns by aligning inputs and outputs at each scale; (2) scale-wise autoregression, where coarse-scale predictions guide finer-scale forecasting through hierarchical information flow; and (3) a modular architecture, enabling seamless integration with diverse backbones such as CNNs, MLPs, and Transformers. Extensive experiments across a broad set of datasets and forecasting models demonstrate that MSAR achieves consistent improvements in both accuracy and inference efficiency, validating the effectiveness of scale-aligned autoregression for multiscale time series forecasting. The code is available at: https://github.com/Oryxo/MSAR.

title: SpeCal: Spectral Calibration for Unsupervised RLVR
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has substantially improved the reasoning abilities of large language models, but its dependence on ground-truth answers or external verifiers limits its ability to exploit abundant unlabeled reasoning data. Unsupervised RLVR alleviates this bottleneck by deriving scalar rewards from the model's own rollouts. However, the reliability of such self-generated supervision varies substantially across rollout groups and individual responses, while existing methods construct or refine their rewards mainly from decoded outcomes and reward statistics. These endpoint signals reveal what answers the model produces, but provide limited information about whether the underlying rollout representations form a reliable structure for learning. Our key observation is that hidden-state spectra offer a complementary view of supervision reliability by characterizing both the organization of a rollout group and the support received by each rollout within that group. Based on this observation, we propose SpeCal, a bi-level spectral calibration framework for unsupervised RLVR. At the group level, SpeCal combines spectral mass with a Gaussian band-pass gate over normalized entropy-based effective rank, favoring rollout groups with substantial representation variation whose effective dimensionality lies in a preferred regime. At the rollout level, the same group effective rank determines how many dominant directions are retained in a leave-one-out spectral subspace formed by the remaining rollouts, within which the conditional support of each held-out rollout is measured. The resulting signals calibrate the original reward-induced advantages at the group and rollout levels without redefining the underlying unlabeled reward.

title: MASTA: A Feedback-Scheduled Multi-Agent System for End-to-End Tamarin Modeling and Analysis
abstract: Tamarin-based formal verification of security protocols requires expert-authored multiset rewriting rules and temporal-logic lemmas. Translating a natural-language protocol description into a complete formal model with an LLM is hard because syntactic, reachability, and property-level errors compound across the multi-step modeling process, and a single agent that both authors and self-evaluates cannot reliably localize them. We present MASTA, a multi-agent system that addresses these difficulties through three innovations. First, an operational--evaluative role decomposition assigns rule modeling to an Architect, property modeling to an Auditor, and pure dispatch to a dedicated Arbiter that holds no authoring duties. Second, the Arbiter implements a Tamarin-anchored scheduler that dispatches the next agent based on the latest verifier verdict and routes problem-tagged fixes through a modification list, with a six-class problem taxonomy and an LLM deduplication check preventing routing deadlock. Third, we construct a benchmark of 10 protocols paired with 139 mutation variants and five fine-grained metrics that jointly assess model correctness ($M_1$--$M_3$) and completeness ($M_4$--$M_5$). On this benchmark, MASTA on Qwen 3.5-plus improves over OpenCode on the same backbone by up to $+0.27$ on individual metrics and ranks first on both the correctness and completeness averages, surpassing Codex (GPT-5.5) and Claude Code (Opus 4.7) despite using a weaker LLM. Ablations on five protocols confirm that removing the Arbiter collapses property and verification scores to zero.

title: Instrumenting Failure: Scoring Language Model Agents at Every Decision Node in Imperfect-Information Games
abstract: Agent evaluations report task success and rarely say what an agent did at each decision. We score every decision node of three 12B to 14B instruct-tuned language models (LMs) playing five zero-sum imperfect-information games against four opponents on eight properties from decision and game theory, five of them against a CFR+ equilibrium reference. At each node, the LM also states a belief about the opponent's hidden state in a separate call. Without memory and at temperature 0, stated beliefs sit 0.250 to 0.288 in total variation distance from the equilibrium posterior, and where the action responds to the state its agreement with that belief exceeds chance by -0.04 to 0.19. The two calls frame the opponent differently, so the result is a behavioural inconsistency and makes no claim about internal beliefs. Under one prompt and greedy decoding, the LM's action never varies with the state in 10 of the 38 cells where the reference varies its own. Memory lowers the constant-action share in 9 of 13 testable ladders at temperature 0; at temperature 0.2 the cells at 1 fall from 16 to 5 of the 46 informative cells, while the belief results hold. A gate withholds, with a stated reason, any belief score the run cannot support, and seven of the eight non-zero defect rates are attributable to the instrument, a representation, or the LMs.

title: Contrastive Activation-Guided Zeroth-Order Preference Optimisation for Memory-Efficient LLM Alignment
abstract: Direct Preference Optimisation (DPO) simplifies reinforcement learning from human feedback, but still relies on traditional backpropagation and its associated activation-memory cost. Zeroth-order (ZO) optimisation avoids backpropagation, yet isotropic perturbations can produce noisy updates for preference objectives defined by differences between chosen and rejected responses. We introduce Contrastive Activation-guided Zeroth-Order Direct Preference Optimisation (CA-ZODPO), which constructs a low-rank search subspace from the activation discrepancy between the chosen and rejected responses in each preference pair. Perturbations are restricted to this subspace, while momentum is maintained in low-rank coordinates to preserve the memory advantages of ZO training. On Qwen2.5-1.5B with Anthropic HH-RLHF, CA-ZODPO outperforms common ZO baselines and remains competitive with first-order DPO in pairwise preference evaluation.
